Eleva Care · design audit · 2026-11-14

Where the design is weak, and what to build instead

Every key screen was captured on desktop and phone, reviewed by a six-seat panel, and matched to patterns from shipped products on Mobbin. Audit of 2026-11-14 with its plan. By 2026-11-21, 18 of the first 39 slices are merged (D0.1 to D0.3, D1.1 to D1.5, D2.1, D2.2, D5.7 to D5.9, D7.1 to D7.5); the 21 still open, and the three of Phase 8, are listed in execution-plan/remaining-roadmap.md. On 2026-11-23 the public site became its own track (Track E, the marketing thread) and the founder opened its whole design for a rethink: Phase 8 holds the new slices, and D3, D2.3, D2.4 and D6.1 are built in that track against the seven-seat panel in judges-panel.md.

Seven moves that change the most

The panel's 49 P1 findings cluster into these. Each chip opens the finding with its evidence and references.

  1. 1

    Rebuild the pay step as a confirm-and-pay page, in a quiet checkout frame

    The money moment is the thinnest screen in the product: no price breakdown, nothing reassuring beside the button, and the whole funnel sits inside the marketing header and a forty-link footer.

    BOOK-01BOOK-02BOOK-03TRUST-03TRUST-06

  2. 2

    Turn the checked registration into visible proof, on the profile and on every expert card

    It is the one fact Eleva verifies about an expert, and today it reads as grey small print.

    PROF-01TRUST-04DISC-05

  3. 3

    Give every profile a person: photo rule, profession line, approach, first session

    A member is choosing someone to trust with her health. Without a photo and a structured story the page is a monogram and a price.

    PROF-02PROF-03DISC-02DISC-03

  4. 4

    Put real, bookable experts and a need-first entry on the homepage and the explorer

    The homepage never shows an expert a member can book, and neither page lets her start from what she needs.

    HOME-01HOME-02HOME-03DISC-01

  5. 5

    Give experts a door, then rebuild setup as one focused, profile-first journey

    A professional who signs up lands on a member Space with no way in. Setup then opens with a tax number and never shows her the profile she is building.

    AUTH-01ONB-01ONB-02ONB-03ONB-05

  6. 6

    Make the two home pages answer a question

    Expert Today should say what needs her today and whether she can be paid. Member home should feel like a companion, not an empty admin panel.

    XDASH-01XDASH-02XDASH-04MEM-01

  7. 7

    Explain each trust moment in one plain sentence, where it is asked

    The legal substance is complete, but the health-data consent is a bare link and the privacy page is five identical Grant buttons.

    TRUST-01TRUST-02MEM-02BOOK-04

Method

How each slice is designed and judged

The same loop for every design challenge from now on. Mobbin sets the bar, and the Eleva voice stays. In the signed-in product the logo, palette and type stay too. On the public site the founder opened the whole design for a rethink on 2026-11-23: Awwwards winners join the references and a seven-seat panel judges (judges-panel.md).

  1. Search Mobbin

    Search for the slice's problems and add what teaches something to _context/mobbin/library/{surface}/references.json.

  2. Capture before

    Run the capture spec if the surface changed since 2026-11-14-before.

  3. Design and build

    One slice, against the findings it closes and the references they cite.

  4. Capture after

    Same spec, new label. This page then shows before and after side by side.

  5. Judges panel

    Three judges score out of 10: UI and visual design; UX and UX writing; trust, legal, compliance and accessibility. Each reads the after captures against the surface's criteria with the references open. The public site has seven blind seats: an Awwwards jury seat (design 40%, usability 30%, creativity 20%, content 10%), UI, UX, UX writing, GDPR, compliance and accessibility, and security.

  6. Pass or revise

    A slice ships only when every judge scores 8.5 or more and its P1 findings are closed. Otherwise it is revised and judged again. Anything marked for legal review also goes to a lawyer before launch.

Capture command: E2E_DESIGN_CAPTURE=1 E2E_SKIP_WEBSERVER=1 E2E_ALLOW_DB_WRITES=1 DESIGN_CAPTURE_LABEL={date}-{slice} pnpm exec playwright test e2e/design-capture.spec.ts --project=chromium --workers=1, then node docs/eleva-v3/design-audit/build.mjs.

01-homepage · Marketing and brand

Public homepage

The homepage looks calm and well made, and the headline says what Eleva is in one line, but it never shows a member a single expert they can book: the only named faces are advisors, and the route to a real expert is one generic button. Proof is thin (four two-word labels, no member voice, no numbers) and the page ends on a pitch to experts. The change that matters most is to put the choice of need and a row of real, bookable experts in the first two screens, and move the advisors below them as supporting proof.

3 P18 P22 P325 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

Captures

Home
Home scroll (video)

Keep

  • The headline 'Women's health experts, on your schedule.' plus the lead line answers what Eleva is and who it is for in under ten seconds. Keep both.
  • Lora headings on cream with deep teal read as calm and premium, not clinical. The type scale and spacing are consistent from section to section.
  • The board of advisors is real proof: named people with credentials and a quote. Few health marketplaces at this stage have that.
  • 'No waiting lists and no account needed to book' is a strong, concrete promise, and the three steps are written in plain words.
  • One label, 'Find an expert', is used in the header, the hero and on mobile, so the main action is never renamed.
  • The 'Grow your practice with Eleva' band is clearly for a different audience: its own block, its own coral button, at the end of the page.

Findings

P1HOME-01uxNo bookable expert appears anywhere on the homepageD3.1

What is weak. The page shows eight advisors by name and face, and zero experts a member can book. A first-time visitor reads the advisor portraits as 'these are the experts', then the lead tells her 'Your care comes from the independent expert you choose', and the page never shows who that could be. Reaching one real person takes Find an expert, then the directory, then a profile. For a marketplace the supply is the product; hiding it makes the page feel like a brochure and is the main reason it reads as weak.

Do instead. Add a 'Meet our experts' row directly under the value strip: four to six real expert cards with photo, name, profession, languages, how they meet (video, phone, in person), price from, and the next free slot, each linking to the profile, plus 'See all experts'. On a phone make it a horizontal scroll so a card and a half is visible. Design the card for a new expert with no photo and a short bio (initials on a brand tint, profession and languages still carry the card). Rotate by category so every profession gets shown.

Evidence: home-scroll.desktop.webm

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0301-homepage/0401-homepage/1501-homepage/16

P1HOME-02uxThe hero offers one generic button and no way to start from a needD3.1

What is weak. A member arrives with a need (pelvic pain after birth, breastfeeding, menopause), but the hero gives her only 'Find an expert'. The category chips sit two screens down on desktop and about four screens down on a phone, after three full-width advisor portraits. The two photo cards beside the hero ('Care for every stage of life', 'Experts who listen') look like navigation but are captions that link to /experts/wellness and /experts, and they disappear on mobile.

Do instead. Let the member say what she needs inside the hero. Either a single search field ('What do you need help with?') with the nine categories as suggestions, or a row of five or six need chips under the lead line that go straight to the filtered directory. Replace the two caption cards with need tiles that name a real destination (Pregnancy and postpartum, Pelvic health, Menopause). Keep 'Find an expert' as the fallback button.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0101-homepage/0201-homepage/1201-homepage/13

P1HOME-03trustProof is four short labels; no member voice, no numbers, no word on how experts are checkedD3.2

What is weak. The strip under the hero reads 'Independent experts', 'Online or in person', 'In your language', 'Clear prices'. Each is a claim with nothing behind it, set in small text with wide gaps, so it is easy to miss. The page has no member story, no count of experts or professions, and it never says that Eleva checks each expert's professional registration, which the become-expert page does say. A woman deciding whether to pay a stranger for health care needs exactly that sentence.

Do instead. Turn the strip into four claims with substance, for example 'Every expert's professional registration is checked before they go live', 'Video, phone or in person', 'Sessions in English, Portuguese and Spanish', 'You see the price before you book'. Add a short 'Who you will meet' block with honest figures (experts live, professions covered, advisors on the board) and link it to the trust page. When members consent, add two or three short stories tagged by need. Use real numbers only; a small true number beats none.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0501-homepage/0801-homepage/0201-homepage/1401-homepage/1501-homepage/1901-homepage/20

P2HOME-04uiAdvisors come before the offer and are told twiceD3.2

What is weak. The board of advisors is the first section after the hero, ahead of the services, and the same authority returns four sections later as a full-width teal quote from Kari Bø. On a phone the three advisor portraits stack at full width (roughly 1,200px of scrolling) before a member sees what she can book. The advisors are strong proof, but in this position they delay the offer and blur who delivers the care.

Do instead. Merge the two sections into one compact band placed after the experts and services: the lead advisor's quote with her portrait, a row of the other seven faces with name and one-line credential, the universities or institutions they come from as a logo line, and 'Meet the board'. On mobile show the quote plus a single row of small faces, not three full-width portraits.

Evidence: home-scroll.mobile.webm

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0601-homepage/07

P2HOME-05uxTwo competing ways to browse: nine profession chips and four life-stage photo cardsD3.2

What is weak. 'Expert-led care, tailored to you' shows nine chips named by profession (Psychology, Midwifery, Lactation...) and under them four stock-photo cards named by life stage (Pregnancy and postpartum, Pelvic health, Through every stage...). They are two taxonomies for the same directory, and neither says what a member will find behind it. The photo cards are the part of the page that looks most like a template, and on a phone they add four tall cards in a column.

Do instead. Use one grid, 'Start from what you need', with six to eight tiles. Each tile names the need in the member's words, lists two or three example services ('Pelvic floor assessment', 'Return to exercise after birth') and shows how many experts offer it. Keep professions as a filter inside the directory. On mobile lay the tiles out two per row, or as one scrolling row.

Evidence: home-scroll.desktop.webm

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0201-homepage/1701-homepage/1801-homepage/13

P2HOME-06ui'How it works' explains the product without showing itD3.2

What is weak. Three numbered text rows sit beside one stock photo of a woman at a laptop. Nothing shows what booking on Eleva looks like, so the section could belong to any service. The strongest line on the page, 'No waiting lists and no account needed to book', is set as grey lead text.

Do instead. Give each step a small piece of the real interface: an expert card for 'Find your expert', the date and time picker for 'Book a time', the confirmation email with its Join button for 'Meet your expert'. Promote 'No account needed to book' into the hero or the value strip, and end the section with a 'Find an expert' button.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/09

P2HOME-07copyThe space under the hero headline is spent on a slogan, a hedge and the other audienceD3.1

What is weak. The eyebrow 'Women's health, elevated' is a slogan that adds no information. The second hero button is 'Become an expert', which gives the most valuable spot on the page to a different audience that already has a nav menu and its own band. The line under the buttons, 'Eleva connects you with independent health experts who run their own practice', reads as a legal hedge where a reassurance should be.

Do instead. Drop the eyebrow or use it for place and language ('Portugal · English, Portuguese, Spanish'). Replace the second button with 'How it works' or with need chips (see HOME-02) and leave expert recruitment to the header and the band. Rewrite the last line as a benefit that still states the model: 'You choose your expert. They run their own practice; Eleva takes care of booking and payment.'

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0101-homepage/0201-homepage/12

P2HOME-08uxOn a phone the page is about 27 screens long and the first screen is only the heroD3.2

What is weak. The mobile capture is 10,566px tall. The hero fills the whole first screen with a dimmed video in which a face sits directly behind the headline, the header carries four unlabelled icons (globe, person, search, menu), and the value strip wraps into an uneven two-by-two block. Advisors, service cards and the how-it-works photo each stack at full width, and the footer alone is about 1,900px.

Do instead. Shorten the mobile hero so the value strip and the top of the next section show on the first screen, and use a still crop that keeps faces clear of the text. Make the strip a tidy two-column grid. Turn advisors, experts and need tiles into horizontal rows. Target under 6,500px in total. Label or reduce the header icons: logo, 'Find an expert', menu.

Evidence: home-scroll.mobile.webm

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/0301-homepage/14

P2HOME-09uxThe page ends on the pitch to experts, with no questions answered and no closing action for membersD3.2

What is weak. The last three blocks are a belief statement ('Women's health is a lifelong journey'), a link to the mission, and 'Grow your practice with Eleva'. A member who has scrolled the whole page still has open questions (what a session costs, how a video session works, whether she can cancel, who the experts are) and the final button she sees is 'Become an expert'.

Do instead. Add a short FAQ before the expert band with five or six questions in the member's words: What is Eleva? Who are the experts and how are they checked? How much does a session cost? How do online sessions work? Can I cancel or reschedule? Do I need an account? Close with a member call to action ('Find an expert') and keep the expert band as the last, clearly separate block. Fold the belief statement into the About page or into one line above the FAQ.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 01-homepage/1001-homepage/2301-homepage/24

P3HOME-10uiThe footer is dominated by fourteen legal links and has no way back into careD3.2

What is weak. The Legal column lists fourteen links and is twice the height of the others. The first column is titled 'Join Eleva' but holds About and Our story. There is no 'Find care' column with the categories, no contact or help line, and no language switch. On a phone the footer is a single list about 1,900px long.

P2HOME-12uiTen unrelated stock photographs and one repeated section layout set the lookD8.1

What is weak. Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 10

02-discovery · Marketplace and profile

Expert explorer (/experts)

The explorer is a warm heading over a grid of cards that say only a name, one free-text line and a price. A member cannot start from her need, cannot compare two experts without opening both, and sees three blank monogram panels where people should be. The change that matters most is the card: give it a face (or a compact layout when there is none), a profession and focus, languages, how and where sessions happen, the next open time and a checked-registration mark, then put areas of care above the grid as the way in.

3 P16 P21 P320 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

Captures

Experts

Keep

  • The heading and lead are in the right voice: "Real people with real training. Pick someone whose work fits you, then meet by video, by phone or in person." Keep them.
  • On phones the card turns into a compact row (small portrait left, text right), so a short list fits in one screen (01-experts.mobile.jpg).
  • Ordering is disclosed. "How we order experts" links to the ranking terms, and the source labels the paid plan honestly ("Top Expert · paid plan", "Top Expert first (paid plan)"). Few marketplaces are this open; make it more visible rather than changing it.
  • The trust line has the right content: "Before a profile goes live, our team checks the expert's professional registration."
  • The whole card is one link and one tab stop, and the free option is said in plain words ("Free session available").
  • The source already has a first-run state for an empty directory with three next steps (newsletter, how Eleva works, are you an expert). The pattern is right; it only needs a design pass.

Findings

P1DISC-01uxA member cannot start from her needD2.4

What is weak. The page opens with a heading and goes straight to people. There is no search field, no areas of care, no mode or language choice. A member arrives with a need (pelvic pain after birth, breastfeeding, anxiety in pregnancy), not with a name. In the source, area chips only appear once two areas have experts, and language and sort only appear from 12 experts, so at launch size the page offers nothing to narrow or even to explain what Eleva covers. The teal search button in the mobile header looks like search but sits in the same slot as the desktop "Find an expert" link, which on this page points back to itself.

Do instead. Put areas of care above the grid from day one as photo or icon tiles with a count ("Pelvic health · 3 experts") and show areas with nobody yet as "Opening soon" rather than hiding them, so the page teaches the catalogue. Add one plain search field ("What do you need help with?") that matches areas, service names and expert names. Keep two always-on chips next to it: language and how you meet (video, phone, in person). Hide the header "Find an expert" button on this page.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 02-discovery/0402-discovery/1202-discovery/0602-discovery/0302-discovery/1602-discovery/2002-discovery/19

P1DISC-02trustCards carry too little to choose onD2.4

What is weak. Each card shows a name, one free-text line and a price. It does not say what the person is (physiotherapist, midwife), what she focuses on, which languages she speaks, whether sessions are by video or in a city, when she is next free, or that her registration was checked. The source can show two areas of care as a quiet line, but only when the expert has picked categories, so a new expert's card falls back to almost nothing. To compare three experts a member has to open three profiles.

Do instead. Fix a card content model with required fields: photo, name with a checked-registration mark, profession and up to two focus areas, languages, how you meet ("Video · In person in Lisboa"), next open time ("Next: Mon 16 Nov") and price from. Make profession and at least one area required before a profile can be listed, so no card depends on a free-text headline. Add a quiet "View profile" affordance; keep the whole card as one link.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 02-discovery/0102-discovery/0202-discovery/0302-discovery/1002-discovery/1402-discovery/19

P1DISC-03uiThe missing-photo placeholder takes over the cardD2.4

What is weak. On desktop each card gives about 290px of its 420px to a pale gradient panel with a monogram circle (AQ, FM, PM). Three of them in a row read as an unfinished page, and the only photograph on the screen belongs to the expert-recruitment band below. New experts will often have no photo on day one, so this is the default look of the directory, not an edge case.

Do instead. Ask for a portrait before a profile can be listed (a publish gate in expert setup, with guidance on a good photo). For any profile that still has none, use the compact layout at every breakpoint: a small avatar beside the text, so the card's weight goes to profession, focus and next time instead of an empty panel. Order profiles with a photo ahead of those without inside the same sort.

P2DISC-04uxFilters cover two of the things members filter onD2.4

What is weak. The captures show no controls because the directory is under 12 experts. Read from the source, the full set is a language select, a sort select and an "Apply filters" button in a grey box. There is no filter for how you meet, location, price or availability, the native selects need a separate submit, and nothing shows how many experts will match. On a phone a form row above the list pushes the first expert down.

Do instead. Use a chip row that applies on tap: area, language, how you meet, city (only when in person is chosen), price, and "Free first chat". Show applied filters as removable chips with a result count ("7 experts"). On phones open one "Filters" bottom sheet with a sticky button that carries the count ("Show 7 experts") and a "Clear all".

P2DISC-05trustChecked registration and ordering are a footnoteD2.1

What is weak. The strongest trust statement on the page, that Eleva checks each expert's professional registration before the profile goes live, is one line of small grey text under the grid, next to the "How we order experts" link. A member choosing someone for her health reads the cards first and may never reach it. Nothing on a card repeats it, and the current order (name A to Z) is not stated anywhere.

Do instead. Move the statement above the grid as a short line with a check icon, and repeat it as a small mark beside each name that opens a one-sentence explanation. State the order next to the count ("3 experts · sorted A to Z") with "How we order experts" beside it. When Top Expert placement is active, label it on the card itself, as the source already does on desktop, and show the same label on phones (today the badge is hidden below the sm breakpoint).

What is weak. The third card (Patricia Mota) has no price row because she has no services yet. It looks like a rendering gap, and tapping it leads to a profile that says she is not taking bookings. In a list of three, one dead end is a third of the experience.

Do instead. List an expert only once one service is published. If the founder wants early profiles visible, label the card "Opening soon", sort it last, and replace the price row with "Tell me when bookings open". For bookable experts fill the same row with the next open time so every card ends on something a member can act on.

What is weak. "Bring your practice to Eleva" is a 470px dark band with the page's only photograph on desktop, and on phones it is about 690px tall, longer than the list of experts above it (about 470px). A member's page ends on a message for someone else, and the strongest visual on the screen is not an expert she can book.

Do instead. End the member's page with help for the member: a short "Not sure who to choose?" block that asks what she needs and suggests an area or a free first chat, with a link to how Eleva works. P2DISC-08uxFew-results and no-results states stop shortD2.4

What is weak. With three experts the page is a heading, one row of cards and white space. Nothing says how many experts there are or that the list is growing. Read from the source, a filter that matches nobody shows "No experts match these filters yet." with a single "See all experts" button, which throws away every choice the member made instead of helping her loosen one.

Do instead. Show a count and frame a short list as chosen ("3 experts, each with a checked registration"). When filters leave few or no results, keep the results visible, list the applied filters as removable chips under "See more experts", and say which one to drop. When an area has nobody yet, offer "Tell me when a [area] expert joins" and the nearest area that does have experts.

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 10

03-profile · Marketplace and profile

Expert public profile (/{username})

The profile's booking mechanics are sound: real next times, a sticky card on desktop, a sticky bar on phones, a cancellation line on every service. What is weak is the person. With no photo, no profession line and a short bio, the page is a monogram, a name and grey small print, and the one fact Eleva has checked (the professional registration) reads like a legal footnote. The change that matters most is to turn that checked registration into a visible proof block beside the name and to give every profile a structured "about" (profession, focus, approach, training, what a first session looks like) that still looks complete when an expert is new. References 25 and 26 (2026-11-21) prepare the clinic's public page: the team shown as people, and choosing a professional or the first one free. References 27 to 34 (2026-11-23) look at the profile as the first step of the booking flow: service rows of one shape, an availability card that asks in order, and a phone bar that opens the time picker.

4 P19 P22 P336 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

Captures

Profile paid
Profile free

Keep

  • Next open times are on the profile itself, grouped by day, with the member's timezone named. On desktop the booking card stays in view while she reads (01-profile-paid.desktop.jpg).
  • Phones already have a sticky bar with the starting price and "See times" (01-profile-paid.mobile.jpg, 02-profile-free.mobile.jpg). Keep it and make it do more.
  • The registration line is real, checkable proof: the professional body links to its public register and the licence number is shown. Few marketplaces offer this. It needs presence, not replacement.
  • Every service states its cancellation window in plain words ("Free cancellation up to 24 hours before"), and the booking card closes with "No account needed".
  • "How I can help" and "About me" are in the expert's own voice, which suits a page about a person.
  • The FAQ asks the right questions ("Who provides my care?", "What does Eleva check?") and answers them honestly.
  • The source already supports a large portrait hero, area-of-care links above the name, a credential line and a "Training and credentials" timeline. They are simply empty for a new expert, so the design problem is the fallback, not the full state.

Findings

P1PROF-01trustThe checked registration reads as small printD2.1

What is weak. "Ordem dos Fisioterapeutas · Licence no. 9115 · ERS registration no. 182844" is one line of 14px grey text between the facts and the share button. Nothing says Eleva checked it, when, or what the numbers mean. "ERS" is unexplained and the body's name is in Portuguese on an English page. The explanation exists, but as the sixth closed item of the FAQ at the bottom ("What does Eleva check?"). A member deciding whether to trust this person with her health has no visible signal that anyone verified anything.

Do instead. Make it a proof block directly under the name: a check icon, "Registration checked by Eleva" with the month it was checked, then the body in plain words ("Registered physiotherapist, Ordem dos Fisioterapeutas, no. 9115") with "View on the public register", and the health regulator registration on its own line with its name written out. Add a small "What we check" link that opens one honest paragraph: Eleva checks the professional registration before a profile goes live; experts describe their own training and experience. Put the same check mark beside the name on the explorer card.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 03-profile/0703-profile/0403-profile/0503-profile/06

P1PROF-02trustThere is little proof of the person beyond a nameD2.2

What is weak. With a two-sentence bio the profile has no years in practice, no focus areas, no approach, no training, no description of a first session and no voice from other members. "About me" sits below every service card, and on phones below the booking card too, about 2,100px down. "What to expect" exists only as a closed accordion inside one service. The free profile has no "About me" at all, so the page goes from one service straight to a booking FAQ. The source has a "Training and credentials" timeline, but an expert who skips it leaves nothing behind.

Do instead. Give the profile a fixed spine that expert setup fills step by step: (1) an at-a-glance row under the header (profession, years in practice, focus areas); (2) "My approach", three or four sentences prompted in setup; (3) "Your first session", three numbered steps the expert edits from a default for her profession; (4) "Training and credentials"; (5) "What members say", shown once an expert has a few reviews from members who completed a session, and a quiet "New on Eleva" tag until then rather than empty stars. Move a two-line version of the bio into the header so it is read before the prices. Ask for approach and at least one training entry before a profile can be published.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 03-profile/0303-profile/0603-profile/0803-profile/1103-profile/12

P1PROF-03uiWithout a photo the header loses the personD2.2

What is weak. The header pairs a 110px monogram circle with a 60px serif name. The monogram looks like an account avatar from a dashboard, not someone you would book. The source shows a 4:5 portrait as the largest element when a photo exists, so a profile with and without one are two different pages, and new experts get the weaker one. Nothing under the name says what she is: the only hint of a profession is the name of the regulatory body in the small print.

Do instead. Ask for a portrait before a profile can be published, with a short guide in setup (face, daylight, plain background) and a crop tool. Add a profession line as the first thing under the name ("Physiotherapist · Pelvic health"), required, taken from the areas of care. For the rare profile still without a photo, keep the full-size 4:5 frame with a branded Eleva illustration and the initials, so the layout and the page's weight stay the same.

Mobbin references: 03-profile/0103-profile/0603-profile/09

P2PROF-04uiHeader facts run together as one grey sentenceD2.2

What is weak. Languages, how you meet, cities and countries served are joined with dots into one paragraph of small grey text. On the free profile the country list names 27 countries and runs four lines on desktop and six on a phone, pushing the first service to about 720px on mobile, below the first screen. The facts a member scans for first (does she speak my language, can I see her in my city) are the hardest to pick out.

Do instead. Break the facts into three short rows with icons: languages, how you meet ("Video, phone" or "Video, in person in Lisboa, Porto and Madrid"), and where members can be. Collapse long country lists ("Members across the EU", with the list behind "See countries"). On phones keep the whole header within one screen so the first service or the first times are visible without scrolling.

What is weak. The mobile order is header, service cards, then the booking card. On the paid profile the booking card starts about 1,450px down with two services; an expert with five services pushes it far further. The sticky bar helps, but it shows only "From €45.00" and "See times", the same label as the button in each service card, and it jumps down the page instead of starting a booking. A member never sees when the expert is next free until she gets there.

What is weak. For an expert with three locations the first day shows "08:00 Madrid, 12:00 Lisboa, 12:00 Porto, 12:00 Madrid, 12:30 Lisboa, 12:30 Porto". P2PROF-07uiService cards are uneven and repeat the same actionD2.3

What is weak. "Follow-up" comes before "First visit", so a new member reads the wrong service first. Follow-up has addresses, an included item and two accordions; First visit has a title, a price and nothing else. Each card has its own "See times" button, the booking card has "See all times" and the phone has a sticky "See times": three controls with nearly the same label and different behaviour. Prices carry cents ("€45.00").

Do instead. Order services with first visits first and tag one "Start here". Require a one-sentence description per service and show it on the card. Use one meta line in sentence case with icons ("45 min · In person · Lisboa, Porto, Madrid") and keep full addresses behind "See addresses". Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 12

04-booking-checkout · Booking and checkout

Public booking funnel and checkout

The funnel is short, honest and already carries a summary card, a time zone line, a dated cancellation deadline and a hold on the slot, so the bones are right. It feels weak because the money moment is thin: the pay step has no real order summary, no reassurance beside the button and a hold timer that scrolls away on a phone, while the step before it asks for five ticks and the whole thing sits inside the marketing header and a forty-link footer. The one change that matters most is to rebuild the pay step as a confirm-and-pay page: one order summary (who, what, when, price, dated cancellation), the hold and the reassurance next to the button, promo and tax number tucked into the summary, in a quiet checkout chrome. Note: capture 01-paid-funnel-entry shows the time step, because the seeded paid service has one way to meet and the funnel skips the meet step, so the meet step was not audited. References 23 to 34 (2026-11-23) cover the journey as a flow: what carries forward between steps, one frame for every step on a phone, where the promo code and the wallet button sit, the seconds after paying, and what a guest can still change on the thank-you page.

Keep

  • A summary card travels with every step and already holds expert, service, duration, way of meeting, chosen time, price and one cancellation line (01-paid-funnel-entry.desktop.jpg, 07-paid-step-pay.desktop.jpg). Keep it and make it work harder.
  • The funnel is short: three steps for a paid session, and the meet step is skipped when there is only one way to meet. 'Step 1 of 3' plus a segmented bar is clear without being loud.
  • The time step shows several days at once, says which time zone the times are in with a 'Change time zone' link, and the continue button repeats the choice: 'Continue with Mon, 16 Nov, 10:00' (04-paid-slot-picked.desktop.jpg). On phones that button is a fixed bar.
  • The cancellation policy is turned into real dates for this booking: 'Full refund if you cancel before 15 Nov 2026, 10:00' (05-paid-step-details.desktop.jpg). That sentence is the best line in the funnel.
  • Guests are never asked to create an account before booking, and the thank-you page says 'No account needed' for joining the call (09-free-thank-you.desktop.jpg).
  • The pay button names the amount ('Pay €60.00'), MB WAY sits beside card for Portuguese members, and the source already has a 'Keep this time for 5 more minutes' offer when the hold is about to end.
  • The thank-you page appears with a 'What happens next' list, an add-to-calendar button and the account invitation together, with no delay.
  • The free path skips payment and renames the button to 'Confirm booking'.
  • Headings are warm and plain ('Pick a time', 'A few details'), and the urgent-help note is a responsible thing for a health product to carry.

Findings

P1BOOK-01uxCheckout runs inside the full marketing siteD1.1

What is weak. Every step keeps the marketing header (four mega menus, Sign in, a filled 'Find an expert' button) and the full footer with about forty links. On the time step the footer is taller than the step itself, and on a phone the pay button is followed by a screen and a half of footer links. A member who is about to pay is shown a dozen ways to leave, and 'Find an expert' is the strongest button on the page while she is already booking one. It also makes the page read as a website form rather than a checkout.

Do instead. Give the funnel its own quiet chrome from the first step to the thank-you page: the Eleva logo (returns to the expert's profile), the language switch, a 'Help' link and a small lock with 'Secure booking'. Replace the footer with one line: Terms, Privacy, Cookie settings and the company name. Keep the real header and footer on the profile page before the funnel and on the pages after it.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/0104-booking-checkout/02a04-booking-checkout/09a

P1BOOK-02uiThe pay step has no order summary or price breakdownD1.2

What is weak. On the pay step the price is shown twice with no relation between the two: 'Price €60.00' in the side card and a small 'Total' label with '€60.00' floating on the next line at the far right of the form. There is no line that says what the €60 buys, no 'you pay today', no tax note, and a discount has no visible home until a code is applied. On a phone the side card sits above the form and is gone by the time the card fields are on screen, so the member types her card number with nothing on screen that says what she is paying for. This is the main reason the checkout reads as weak.

Do instead. Make the side card the order summary and the only place the money is shown. Lines: 'First visit, 60 minutes, video with Fisio Mota'; 'Mon 16 Nov, 10:00 to 11:00 (Lisbon time)' with a Change link; a price line; a discount line when a code is applied; 'Total you pay today'; and the dated cancellation sentence. Remove the loose Total row from the form. On phones keep a fixed bottom bar with 'Total €60.00' and the pay button, and let the total open the full summary.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/02a04-booking-checkout/0304-booking-checkout/0404-booking-checkout/0504-booking-checkout/23a04-booking-checkout/24a

P1BOOK-03trustNothing reassures the member next to the pay buttonD1.2

What is weak. Between the last field and 'Pay €60.00' the only text is Stripe's Link terms. There is no line about payment security, no reminder that she can cancel for a full refund until a named date, and nothing about what happens the moment she pays. The intro sentence hedges: 'Card, Apple Pay, Google Pay, Link, and MB WAY may appear' reads like a note to a developer. At the point of most doubt the page is silent.

Do instead. Rewrite the intro: 'We are holding Monday 16 November at 10:00 for you. Pay by card, Apple Pay, Google Pay or MB WAY.' Directly under the pay button add three short lines with small icons: 'Secure payment. Your card details go straight to Stripe, our payment partner.' (wording to confirm), 'Full refund if you cancel before Sun 15 Nov, 10:00.' and 'Your confirmation and join link arrive by email right away.' For request-to-book services, put the existing 'the expert accepts within 24 hours, a decline refunds 100%' sentence here too.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/0104-booking-checkout/0404-booking-checkout/0304-booking-checkout/24a

P1BOOK-04uxFive ticks and a policy box stand between the member and paymentD1.3

What is weak. The 'Policy and consent' card stacks a five-line cancellation box, an institutional intro ('To book a health session on this digital health platform, please confirm:'), four required checkboxes of equal weight and a fifth, optional one that is a four-line paragraph about transcription and AI notes. On a phone this is a full screen of small text and five tap targets about 16px wide. The optional AI choice is the longest item and looks like one more thing she must read to book. The continue button stays washed out until all four are ticked and nothing says why.

Do instead. Keep it lawful and lighter, with legal review before it ships (the consent version and the 'confirm all four statements' error change with it). (1) Keep consent to health data processing as its own unticked checkbox, because it must be an explicit, separate act, and word it by purpose: 'I agree that Eleva and my expert use the health information I share to provide this session.' (2) Fold terms, privacy notice and the 18-or-older, booking-for-myself confirmation into one sentence directly above the button with links, or at most one second checkbox. (3) Move the optional transcription and AI choice out of the booking gate: ask it in the waiting room before the call, or show it as a clearly separate 'Optional' switch with a one-line label and a 'Learn more' link. (4) Make checkbox rows full-width tap targets, 44px tall. (5) Leave the button active and, on press, point at the item that is missing.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/09a04-booking-checkout/0304-booking-checkout/02a

P2BOOK-05copyThe cancellation policy is said three times, and the clearest version is lastD1.3

What is weak. The side card says 'Full refund if you cancel at least 24 hours before the session.' The policy box then gives three generic rules and two dated ones that repeat the first two. The member reads five lines to learn one fact. On phones the side card drops the cancellation line altogether, and on the pay step, where it matters most, the dated version is not shown at all.

Do instead. Lead with the dated sentence everywhere: 'Free cancellation until Sun 15 Nov, 10:00 (Lisbon time). After that, the session is not refunded.' Put it in the summary card on every step (phones included) and under the pay button. Move the generic rules, the 24-hour grace period and the policy name behind a 'Full policy' link that opens in place.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/02a04-booking-checkout/0104-booking-checkout/0404-booking-checkout/27a

P2BOOK-06uxThe hold timer is out of sight when it matters and sounds like a systemD1.2

What is weak. 'Hold expires in 04:42' lives in a pale blue pill inside the side card. On a phone that card is at the top of the page, so the countdown is off screen while the member fills in her card. The wording is about the system's hold, not about her time, and the blue pill is a colour used nowhere else in the funnel. The expired state in the source is a bare sentence and a button.

Do instead. Say it as a promise and keep it in view: 'We are holding your time for 04:42' directly above the payment methods on desktop and inside the fixed pay bar on phones. Keep it calm (teal on cream) until the last minute, then switch to the existing 'Need more time?' offer. When the hold ends, show a card that names the time that was released, says her details are saved, and offers 'See open times'.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 04-booking-checkout/0104-booking-checkout/26

P2BOOK-07uxAn open promo code box is the first thing on the pay stepD1.2

The cue that more days exist is a clipped sixth column. On a phone the summary card, step label, title and time zone line push the first time to the bottom of the first screen, only three days fit, and the day arrows are gone. On phones switch to a row of day chips (empty days greyed and not tappable, the month named above) with the chosen day's times below in a two or three column grid grouped Morning, Afternoon, Evening. On desktop keep the week columns but align rows by time and write 'No times' in an empty day. Put a 'Next available: Mon 16 Nov, 10:00' shortcut above the picker. P2BOOK-16uxSlot-taken, hold-ended and payment-failed states are plain textD1.5

What is weak. These states were not captured; this is read from the funnel source and its strings. A taken slot shows a red strip above the picker ('That time was just taken. Please pick another.'). An ended hold replaces the payment form with one sentence and a button. A declined payment says 'Pick a time again to retry', which sends the member back two steps. Each of these is the moment a member is most likely to give up, and each is handled as an error message, not as a next step.

Do instead. Design them as states of the step. Slot taken: stay on the time step, name the time that went, and highlight the nearest open times on the same day. Hold ended: a card that says her details are saved and offers 'See open times'. Payment declined: stay on the pay step with the hold intact where possible, say nothing was charged, and offer another method. Capture all three for the next audit.

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 11

05-auth · Onboarding and activation

Sign in and sign up

The identifier-first flow is clean, short and on brand on desktop, and should be kept. Its weak points are at the edges: sign-up speaks only to members so a health professional sees no door, the phone layout drops every reassurance the desktop panel carries, and the two 'check your email' screens leave people waiting with nothing to do. The change that matters most is an expert variant of sign-up that carries intent into setup, with a compact trust line on mobile. References 12 and 13 (2026-11-21) prepare the return of people who had an account before the move: setting a new password with the account named, and a disconnected calendar with one button to reconnect.

2 P15 P23 P313 Mobbin referencesAfter: not built yet

Captures

Login
Login step two
Signup
Signup step two
Verify email
Magic link sent

Keep

  • Identifier-first is done properly: one email field or Google first, then a second step that shows the address as a chip with 'Change' (02-login-step-two, 04-signup-step-two). Keep this structure.
  • The desktop brand panel has real presence: deep teal, the Lora headline with a rotating care area, and concrete points such as 'Online, by phone or in person'.
  • The Google button follows Google's branding and sits first; a passkey option and 'Email me a sign-in link instead' are both present without crowding the screen.
  • The magic-link screen states the expiry in plain words ('It works for 5 minutes') and offers 'Use a different email'.
  • Copy is short, warm and in second person ('Almost there. Tell us your name and choose a password.').
  • Password fields have a show/hide control, and the resend button counts down instead of failing silently.

Findings

P1AUTH-01uxSign-up speaks only to members; a health professional has no doorD4.1

What is weak. 'Join Eleva. Book experts and keep your care in one place.' and a panel reading 'Expert care for pregnancy' tell a physiotherapist or midwife that this form is for people seeking care. There is no line for someone who wants to offer it, on sign-up or sign-in, and every new account is then sent to a member Space (see ONB-01 in 06-expert-onboarding). The expert side of the marketplace starts with a moment of doubt on its first screen. Two-sided products keep one form but name both sides: Upwork changes the headline per role and links to the other ('Here to hire talent? Join as a Client'); Preply puts 'Sign up as a student or Sign up as a tutor' directly under 'Log in'.

Do instead. Keep one identifier-first form. Under it add 'Are you a health professional? Join as an expert'. That link, and every link from /become-expert, opens the same form in an expert variant: headline 'Offer care on Eleva', a sub-line about running a practice, and panel points written for experts (get paid through Stripe, your own booking page, members in three languages). The variant carries intent=expert so the account opens practice setup after verification instead of the member Space. On sign-in, add the same two links for people who landed on the wrong page.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0405-auth/05

P1AUTH-02trustOn a phone, all brand reassurance disappearsD4.4

What is weak. The brand panel is hidden below the desktop breakpoint, so the phone screens are a logo, about 170 px of empty cream, and a form. The three trust points, the headline and any sense of what Eleva is are gone. Most members reach sign-up on a phone, from an expert profile or a confirmation email, and are about to hand over an email address for a health service. The empty band also pushes the form down, so on step two the 'Create account' button is likely to sit under the keyboard. Health and wellness apps keep one image or one promise above the buttons on mobile (Google Health), or a short reassurance and the legal line right at the form (Stardust).

Do instead. On mobile, move the form up to sit directly under the logo and add a compact reassurance in the freed space: one Lora line under the heading on the first step ('Care from verified health experts, in your language') and a single row of the three points below the form in small text. Keep it to the first step; steps two and three stay bare so the keyboard never covers the button. Test at 390 x 844 with the keyboard open.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/1005-auth/1105-auth/03

P2AUTH-03uiThe brand panel has no people in itD4.4

What is weak. The panel is a gradient, a headline and three ticks. It is handsome, but a care service earns trust through people: the experts a member will meet, or a member's own words. The third point ('Sessions, payments and privacy settings in one place') lists features rather than a feeling of safety. The rotating word is also caught mid-fade in two captures (01-login and 06-magic-link-sent), leaving 'Expert care for' above an empty or blurred line; check that a word is always legible and that the animation stops under reduced-motion settings. lululemon gives its sign-up a photo of members with one promise; Fiverr surrounds its form with named portraits of the people on the platform.

Do instead. Keep the teal gradient and the Lora headline. Add one human element that rotates with the word: a small expert card (portrait, name, profession, a 'Verified' mark) or a one-sentence member quote with first name and city. Use real, consented photos only; until they exist, use the quote form. Replace the third point with a privacy promise in plain words ('Your health details stay between you and your expert'). Consider a different panel for sign-in (welcome back, your next session) and sign-up (what you get).

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0105-auth/02

P2AUTH-04uxThe two 'check your email' screens are dead endsD4.4

What is weak. After sign-up or a link request the only control is a disabled 'Resend in 30s' button, drawn like a primary action. There is no button to open the inbox, no word about the spam folder, no sender name or subject to look for, and no help link. 'Verify your email' has no way to correct a mistyped address (the magic-link screen does). The address runs inside the sentence and breaks mid-word ('design-' / 'capture...'), so a long address is hard to check. This is the step where a new account is most easily lost. Klaviyo puts the address on its own bold line with 'Update Email' and an 'Open in Gmail' button; Customer.io lists what to check, including the sender and subject line; Reddit's mobile screen keeps a full-width 'Open Email App' with the resend timer as a quiet line above it.

Do instead. Rebuild both screens on one pattern: heading, the address alone on a bold line with 'Change' beside it, then one primary action ('Open Gmail' or 'Open Outlook' when the domain is known; 'Open email app' on mobile). Under it, one helper line: 'Look for an email from Eleva Care. If it is not there in a minute, check spam.' Make resend a text link with the countdown. Keep 'It works for 5 minutes'. Add 'Need help?' to support.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0705-auth/0805-auth/09

P2AUTH-05uiThe 'Check your inbox' screen sits off its column on both viewportsD4.4

What is weak. On desktop the block starts about 160 px left of where every other step starts (x 695 against 855), so it no longer lines up with the form it replaced, and 'Use a different email' is centred under the shifted block. On mobile the logo and text touch the left edge of the screen with no gutter, while every other mobile capture has 20 px. The step animation is vertical, so this is not a transition frame; the likely cause is the long unbroken email address forcing the column wider than its container and scrolling the pane sideways. A real member with a long address would see a visibly broken page at the moment she is deciding whether the email was sent. This is a defect, so no Mobbin reference is needed; the layout fix is the address on its own line as in Klaviyo.

Do instead. Let the description wrap anywhere (overflow-wrap: anywhere, min-width: 0 on the flex child) and put the address on its own truncating line. Add a visual test with a 45-character address at 390 px and 1440 px for the verify and magic-link steps.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/07

P2AUTH-06uxSign-up takes three steps and insists on a passwordD4.4

What is weak. A new member enters an email, then a name and a password, ticks a box, and is then sent to her inbox to verify. Sign-in already offers a link by email, but sign-up does not, so the person least committed to Eleva is asked for the most. A password is one more thing to invent on a phone, and the verification email is going out anyway. Reddit's link screen states the benefit outright ('for you to log in without a password'); lululemon keeps step two to the address, one password field and its rule.

Do instead. On step two, keep the name and offer two ways forward: 'Email me a link' as the first action (one email both verifies the address and signs her in) and 'Use a password instead', which reveals the password field. Members who want a password can add one later in settings. If the product must keep a password at sign-up, at least skip the separate verify screen by signing her in from the verification link.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0905-auth/01

P2AUTH-07uxNo language switch, help link or legal links on the sign-in screensD4.4

What is weak. The panel promises care 'In English, Portuguese and Spanish', yet nothing on the page lets a Portuguese member change the language of the form she is reading. There is no 'Need help?' for someone locked out before a session, and Terms and Privacy appear only on sign-up. On a phone the page has no footer at all. Deel puts 'Have questions? Contact support' and a language menu in the top corner of its login; Preply keeps language and help in the header of the log-in page.

Do instead. Add a small language menu (EN, PT, ES; it sets ELEVA_LOCALE) and 'Need help?' in the top right of the form side on desktop and next to the logo on mobile. Put Terms and Privacy in a quiet footer line on every auth screen.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0605-auth/05

P3AUTH-08uxFour ways to sign in and no memory of which one she usedD4.4

What is weak. Across two steps a returning member can choose Google, a password, an emailed link or a passkey. Someone who joined with Google and now types her email meets a password field she never set. Nothing hints at the method she used last time. Deel's login says 'Log in with your last method or choose another' and shows that method first; Stardust tells returning people to 'use the sign in method you have used in the past'.

Do instead. Remember the last successful method on the device and mark it ('Last used') on the first step. On step two, when the account has no password, lead with 'Email me a sign-in link' and show the Google button instead of an empty password field.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/0605-auth/11

P3AUTH-09uiInput fields look heavy and slightly disabledD4.4

What is weak. Fields are filled with a mid beige and outlined in dark grey, which is the usual look of a disabled control, and the placeholder ('you@example.com') is low contrast on that fill. The 'Sign in' button on step two is drawn in a paler teal than 'Continue' on step one in the desktop capture, and 'Sign in with a passkey' is pale grey text that is easy to miss. No Mobbin reference is needed; lululemon's white field with a clear focus ring shows the conventional treatment.

Do instead. Use a white or near-white field with a 1 px warm border, keep the teal focus ring, and reserve the beige fill for disabled fields. Check placeholder and passkey-link text against 4.5:1. Use one teal for every enabled primary button.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 05-auth/01

P3AUTH-10copyConsent and password guidance are inconsistent between the two sign-up pathsD4.4

What is weak. With Google, agreement is a sentence ('By continuing with Google, you agree to the Terms and Privacy Policy'); with email, it is a checkbox she must tick. The same promise is asked for in two ways one screen apart. The password rule is a single static line ('At least 8 characters.') with no feedback as she types. 'Verify your email' ends with 'Open it to finish creating your Space', the first time the word Space appears in sign-up, with no hint of what it is. lululemon states the password rule under the field and uses one consent sentence under the button; Upwork uses a checkbox for every path.

Do instead. Pick one consent pattern for both paths with legal (a sentence under the button if a checkbox is not required; a checkbox on both if it is). Turn the password line into a live check that ticks when met. Introduce Space once on sign-up ('Your Space is your private home on Eleva: sessions, payments and privacy settings').

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 8

06-expert-onboarding · Onboarding and activation

Expert onboarding: from a new account to a working practice

The wizard is calm and honest, but it is an admin form: it opens with a tax number, never asks who the expert is, and never shows her the profile she is building. It also sits inside a dashboard whose every link sends her back to the form, and a new account that came to offer care lands on a member Space with no visible way in. The change that matters most is to rebuild setup as one focused, full-screen journey in profile-first order (about you, how you see members, first service, licence, payouts, invoices) with a live profile preview, then open the dashboard with a checklist.

Keep

  • The finish step says exactly what happens next in plain words: 'When you finish, we check your licence with your Ordem. Members can book you once it's verified.' Keep this honesty (06-setup-step-5).
  • The licence intro is good trust copy: 'Eleva lists regulated health professionals only. We check these details with your professional body before members can find you.' The 'Why we ask' disclosures are the right instinct (06-setup-step-2).
  • The Online / In person / Phone cards are large, tappable and have a sensible default; they work well on mobile (06-setup-step-1.mobile).
  • The tax number is optional ('You can add it later') and Portugal is preselected and locked in the country list, so nothing blocks a Portuguese expert early.
  • Stripe onboarding is embedded in the page, so the expert never leaves Eleva. The engineering choice is right; only the words around it are weak.
  • The cream, teal and Lora system holds together on every step, and the desktop step rail is easy to read.
  • A hook already exists: the avatar menu offers a shortcut to create an expert workspace when the account has none (packages/dashboard/src/account-menu-model.ts). It only needs to be visible.

Findings

P1ONB-01uxA new account that came to offer care lands on a member Space with no way inD4.1

What is weak. Every sign-up returns to /dashboard and opens the member Space: 'Welcome, Marta', two empty session lists and two 'Find an expert' buttons. Nothing on the page, the sidebar or the mobile header says a health professional can offer care here. The only route is one line inside the avatar menu, or knowing the /account/workspaces URL. A physiotherapist who arrived from /become-expert has just been told she is a member and will reasonably conclude she signed up in the wrong place. This is the gap between 'account created' and 'I am an expert here', and it loses experts before the wizard is ever seen. The repo already holds the fork pattern: _context/mobbin/Apps/web/onboarding/Time2book Web Onboarding/ (Client vs Business) and PoC O6 Path Fork.

Do instead. Carry intent through sign-up: links from /become-expert and the expert sign-up variant (see AUTH-01) add intent=expert, and after verification that account skips the member Space and opens practice setup. For everyone else, add a quiet, dismissible card on the member Space home ('Are you a health professional? Offer care on Eleva') and a permanent 'Offer care on Eleva' link in the sidebar footer and the mobile menu. The card opens a short benefits sheet (three lines and 'Get started'), not the workspace type picker.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 06-expert-onboarding/0106-expert-onboarding/0206-expert-onboarding/12

P1ONB-02uxThe wizard sits inside a dashboard the expert is not allowed to useD4.2

What is weak. The setup form is drawn inside the full practice chrome: Today, Calendar, Services, Members, Public profile, Schedule, Finance and eight more links, with 'Today' highlighted. Until setup is finished every one of them returns to the wizard. The page promises a product and then refuses it twelve times. It also splits attention: a 255 px sidebar, a title column and the form compete on desktop, and on mobile the sidebar toggle opens a menu that goes nowhere. Airbnb, Fresha and Etsy all remove navigation during setup and give it back afterwards.

Do instead. Run the required steps as a focused full-screen flow: logo, 'Save and exit', 'Questions?', one question area, a segmented progress bar and Back / Continue. No sidebar. When the required steps are sent, open the real dashboard with a setup checklist on Today (ONB-12). If the team prefers to let experts look around first, do the opposite consistently: unlock the dashboard read-only and put the checklist on Today. Either works; the current mix of both does not.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 06-expert-onboarding/0106-expert-onboarding/0906-expert-onboarding/10

P1ONB-03uxSetup opens with a tax number and never asks who the expert isD4.2

What is weak. The first question a new expert meets is 'Tax number (NIF)'. The five steps are tax and meeting mode, country and licence, payouts, invoicing, finish. Not one asks her profession, speciality, photo, a line about how she helps, or her first service and price: the things members will see and the reason she joined. Those are pushed to 'Meanwhile you can' cards at the very end. Admin comes first and motivation never arrives, which is the reverse of the Airbnb order the founder wants (tell us about your place, make it stand out, then finish and publish). Etsy places 'How you'll get paid' and billing after naming and stocking the shop for the same reason.

Do instead. Reorder to profile first, money last: 1) About you (profession, speciality, photo; name prefilled). 2) How you see members (online, in person, phone; where you are based; languages). 3) Your first service (name, length, price). 4) Your licence. 5) Get paid (Stripe). 6) Invoices (the NIF belongs here, next to the thing it is used for). 7) Review and send. Steps 1 to 3 build something she can see; 4 to 6 are easier to accept once there is a profile worth protecting.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 06-expert-onboarding/0106-expert-onboarding/0506-expert-onboarding/09

P1ONB-04ux'Where you practise' packs five goals and about twelve controls into one stepD4.2

What is weak. One step asks for practice country, every country she may work in (checkboxes, a second dropdown and an 'Add EU countries' button), languages (checkboxes and another dropdown), professional body, licence number, ERS registration number and a 'Worldwide remote (non-clinical only)' option, with two collapsed 'Why we ask' panels in between. On mobile it is about 1,840 px tall with the button at the very bottom. This is the opposite of one goal per step, and the hardest fields (the licence numbers) arrive buried mid-scroll. 'Clinical modes still follow the countries above' is internal language. The repo's Fresha flow (_context/mobbin/Apps/web/setting up/Fresha Web Setting up an account/) shows the same kind of information asked one question per screen.

Do instead. Split it: 'Where are you based?' with languages on one screen (two answers, both prefilled from locale), and the licence on its own screen (ONB-11). Move 'other countries you may work in' and 'worldwide remote' out of first-run setup into practice settings, reachable from the checklist as 'See members in other countries'. Most Portuguese experts will never need them on day one.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 06-expert-onboarding/0106-expert-onboarding/12

P1ONB-05uxThe expert never sees her public profile taking shapeD4.2

What is weak. On desktop the left third of every step repeats the same static block: 'Set up your practice', 'A few short steps and you're ready to welcome members', a progress card and the step list. It never changes and shows nothing of the result. There is no preview, no 'this is how members will see you', not even a link to the profile. The step list and the card also say the same thing twice ('Step 1 of 5' and '0 of 5 steps complete'). Setup therefore feels like filing paperwork with Eleva instead of opening a practice. The repo already prototyped the answer in PoC O8 Live Preview (_context/PoCs/expert-onboarding/walkthroughs/onboarding-live-preview/) and classic PoC B.

Do instead. Replace the static left column with a live profile card that fills in as she answers: photo or initials, name, profession, languages, how she sees members, first service with price, and a 'Verified by Ordem' slot shown as pending. Empty parts show soft placeholders, so a new expert with no photo still looks deliberate. On mobile, put a 'Preview' button in the header that opens the card as a sheet. Show a full preview before she sends for review.

Mobbin references: 06-expert-onboarding/0406-expert-onboarding/0906-expert-onboarding/11

P1ONB-06trustThe payouts step does not say Stripe, what she will need, or when she gets paidD4.3

What is weak. The whole step is two sentences and a button in an otherwise empty card: 'Complete Payments setup to receive payouts. This stays on this page — no redirects.' and 'Start Payments setup'. It talks about how the page is built, not about her money. It never names Stripe, although the next thing she sees is a Stripe form asking for identity and bank details. It does not say what to have ready (ID document, IBAN), how long it takes, when earnings reach her bank, or what Eleva keeps. The subtitle says 'You can finish this later' but the capture shows no way to do that before starting. Asking for a bank account with this little context is where cautious professionals stop. The repo's PoC S7 (_context/PoCs/expert-onboarding/walkthroughs/setup-stripe-connect/) covers the hand-off mechanics; the missing piece is the framing.

Do instead. Retitle 'Get paid for your sessions'. Before the Stripe form, show a short frame: who (Eleva sends your earnings through Stripe, the payments company; your bank details go to Stripe, not to Eleva staff), what you need (an identity document and your IBAN, about five minutes), when (how soon after a session money arrives) and what Eleva keeps, stated as a plain number. Two buttons: 'Set up payouts' and 'Do this later'. If she skips, the checklist says 'Add your bank account to receive earnings' and members can still be shown the profile once verified, or not, by product rule; say which.

P1ONB-07copyThe invoicing step leads with two greyed-out options and ends on a legal warningD4.3

What is weak. Two of three cards are disabled: TOConline ('Automatic invoice issuance is not active yet') and Moloni ('Coming soon'), each with a faded button. The only working choice is 'Manual invoicing', which asks her to tick 'I understand and accept this invoicing obligation' and press a button labelled 'Acknowledge manual invoicing'. The step reads as unfinished product followed by a liability notice, and it tells the expert what Eleva does not do, which the voice rules forbid. The chips 'PT' and 'PT, ES, BR' are unexplained. No Mobbin reference shows an invoicing-method choice like this one; the closest lesson is Fresha's fees card, which states terms as short, positive facts in one card.

Do instead. Show only what works today. One card: 'You issue your own invoices', one sentence on why (each member needs a certified invoice for a session paid through Eleva, from your own invoicing software), the tax number field moved here from step 1, the checkbox, and a normal 'Continue' button. Remove the disabled provider cards until a provider is live; add them back as real choices then. Drop the country chips or write them out ('Available in Portugal, Spain and Brazil').

P2ONB-08uxTwo step counters back to back: 'Step 2 of 2' with a full bar, then 'Step 1 of 5'D4.1

What is weak. Naming the workspace is labelled 'Step 2 of 2' and its progress bar is already 100% full before she has typed anything. She presses 'Create workspace' expecting to be done and lands on 'Step 1 of 5' with '0 of 5 steps complete'. The finish line moved. An expert should always know how far along she is; here the product tells her twice, differently.

Do instead. Make it one journey with one progress indicator from the type choice to 'send for review'. The practice name becomes an early step of the same flow (or is prefilled and editable inside 'About you'), and the bar only fills for work done. Airbnb's three chapters with a segmented bar and Wise's named stepper, visible from the account-type screen onward, are the models.

What is weak. 'Create a workspace. Choose the type of workspace you want to create.' is a generic SaaS screen. It introduces a third word (workspace) next to Space and practice, gives the three cards equal weight though nearly everyone here is a solo expert, needs two taps (select, then a small 'Continue' that sits below the fold on mobile), and says nothing about what each path involves or whether the choice can be changed. The descriptions are organisational ('Manage multiple experts under one organization') rather than about the person choosing. Here is how to prepare', with the four tasks as real links that tick off, each with a time estimate, plus 'Share your profile link' once verified. On a 390 px screen the eyebrow, 'Set up your practice', the subtitle, the progress card and a row of five numbered circles take the first 380 px on every step, so the actual question starts below the fold each time. Between choosing 'Expert' and the first tax field there is no screen that says how long setup takes, what to have at hand (cédula number, IBAN, tax number), what Eleva keeps from each session, or when members can start booking. The expert learns each requirement only by running into it, which is how the licence and bank steps turn into drop-off points. Airbnb spends one screen on 'It's easy to get started' with three numbered chapters; Whatnot lists fees and rules under 'Here's what to know before you get started'; Fresha shows an 'Overview of fees' card first.

Eleva takes: Title the Stripe step by its benefit, place it after the profile and licence, name the payment partner, confirm what was just saved, and state the rules that matter (timing, fees) before the form.

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 8

07-expert-dashboard · Dashboards

Expert practice dashboard

The expert app is visually calm and on brand, and its editors (schedule, public profile) are clear, but the home page is a counter row plus a list of links that repeat the sidebar. It does not tell an expert what to do today: there is no join action on the next session, no earnings, no share-your-profile prompt, and it stays silent while Finance says payouts are not set up. The one change that matters most is to rebuild Today around a next-session card with Join, a short 'needs you' list (requests, payouts, missing photo) and money at a glance.

Keep

  • Palette, Lora headings and DM Sans body are applied consistently across all ten screens; the app already feels like Eleva, not a generic admin template.
  • The public profile editor teaches while you fill it in: the photo card's 'Works well / Avoid' lists and the 'A bio that helps members choose' guide (05-profile) are the best first-run help in the product and should be the model for other screens.
  • The Finance empty state (07-finance) says what to do, why, how long it takes and that it stays on Eleva. Keep this copy.
  • Weekly hours (04-schedule) are easy to read: one row per day, a checkbox to switch a day off, 'Unavailable' in words, and a plain helper line.
  • The mobile calendar (02-calendar.mobile) switches from a grid to an agenda list with mode icon, time range and service. That is the right mobile pattern.
  • The source already has a 'Waiting for your answer' block with a respond-by date and a licence verification notice on home; the page has the right instincts, it just does not show enough of them.
  • Service rows show a clear Published or Draft pill, price, duration and languages on one line (03-event-types).

Findings

P1XDASH-01uxToday does not answer 'what do I need to do today'D5.1

What is weak. The nav item is called Today, but the page opens with 'Hello, Fisio Mota' and three counters, then 'Next sessions' with rows dated two days ahead. There is no today block, no countdown, and the session rows are static: they are not links and have no Join action (confirmed in apps/expert/src/app/[orgSlug]/page.tsx). Rows show only a first name ('Marta · Online') with no avatar. An expert who opens the app five minutes before a video session has to go to Calendar, find the block and open it to join. This is the core daily path for every expert.

Do instead. Lead the page with one next-session card: member name and initials, service, mode, date and time, a countdown ('Starts in 2 h 10 min'), and a Join session button that is visible from the start and becomes active 15 minutes before, with the reason written under it. Add 'Open member' and 'Reschedule' as quiet secondary actions. Under it, an agenda grouped Today, Tomorrow, Later this week, where every row is a link and every online row carries its own Join. When today is empty, say so in one warm line and show the next booked session instead.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 07-expert-dashboard/0207-expert-dashboard/0507-expert-dashboard/01

P1XDASH-02trustHome stays silent while payouts are not set upD5.1

What is weak. Finance shows 'Set up payouts to get paid', yet the same expert has two published paid services and sessions marked 'Awaiting payment' on home. The single most consequential task for a new expert is hidden under Settings > Finance and the home page gives no sign of it. An expert can take bookings for weeks before learning that her earnings have nowhere to go, which damages trust in the platform at the worst moment.

Do instead. Show a persistent attention banner at the top of Today, and the first row of a 'Needs you' list, until payouts are connected: 'Connect your bank account so your earnings can reach you. It takes a few minutes.' with a Set up payouts button. Repeat the same state as a small coral dot on the Finance nav item. Remove the banner the moment setup completes and confirm with a toast.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 07-expert-dashboard/0307-expert-dashboard/0107-expert-dashboard/04

P1XDASH-03uxNo setup or growth checklist; 'Manage your practice' repeats the sidebarD5.1

What is weak. The lower third of home is four cards (Services, Schedule, Connected calendars, Finance) that link to pages already one click away in the sidebar. They take a full mobile screen and teach nothing. Meanwhile real gaps are visible elsewhere and never surface on home: the profile has no photo and 'No credentials yet' (05-profile), no calendar is connected (09-integrations), payouts are not set up (07-finance). The 08-setup capture resolves to the same home page, so a set-up expert has no view of 'what is next for my practice'.

Do instead. Replace the shortcut cards with a 'Next steps for your practice' checklist driven by real state: add your photo, add your training, connect your calendar, set up payouts, share your profile link. Each row has a one-line reason in member terms ('Members book people, not logos'), a time estimate and one action. Completed rows are ticked and struck through, a progress line shows '3 of 5 done', and the block can be hidden once complete. After setup, swap it for growth prompts (share your link, add a second service, open more hours).

Mobbin references: 07-expert-dashboard/0407-expert-dashboard/01

P1XDASH-04uxNo earnings at a glance and no share-your-profile promptD5.1

What is weak. The three stat cards are 'Sessions this week', 'Requests to review' and 'Published services'. The third is a configuration fact, not something an expert checks daily, and nothing on the page is about money. The only way to the public profile is a 'View public profile' button; there is no link to copy or share, although sharing that link is how a new expert gets her first booking. On mobile the three cards squeeze into narrow columns and the labels wrap to two lines.

Do instead. Use four tiles that answer daily questions: Today (sessions today), Waiting for your answer, Earned this month, Next payout (amount and date, or 'Set up payouts'). Each tile links to its page. Add a profile strip under the greeting with the public address (eleva.care/fisiomota), a Copy link button and View. On mobile, lay tiles out two by two.
