Mobbin references: 07-expert-dashboard/0307-expert-dashboard/0107-expert-dashboard/12

P2XDASH-05uxBooking states are ambiguous and time formats are mixedD5.1

What is weak. Home says 'Requests to review: 0', while the calendar shows five blocks labelled 'Request' on Friday 13, a day that has already passed, drawn in the same style as a live booking. An expert cannot tell whether they still need an answer, have expired or were declined. On home, sessions two days away are 'Awaiting payment' with no hint of what that means for her or whether the time is really held. Home uses 9:00 AM while the calendar and schedule use 09:00.

Do instead. Define one status set and use it everywhere, each with its own colour, icon and plain label: Confirmed, Waiting for your answer (with 'Answer by Thu 14:00'), Waiting for payment (with 'Held until 15:30'), Completed, and Expired or Cancelled (muted and struck through). In the calendar legend, show these states rather than only the session mode. Pick one time format per locale (24-hour for PT and ES) and apply it on home, calendar, schedule and emails.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 07-expert-dashboard/0607-expert-dashboard/05

P2XDASH-06uxDesktop calendar is a mostly empty grid with no actionsD5.4

What is weak. The week view draws fourteen hours for seven days and every event sits in one column. Blocks show time, 'Request' and the service name but not the member's name. Working hours are not shaded, so free time and closed time look the same. There is no Day, Week or List switch and no way to block time or reach the schedule from here. The right rail, the most valuable space next to the grid, is given to a card titled 'ICS feed', a term most physiotherapists and midwives will not know. The line under it, 'Eleva is your calendar. Connect Google or Microsoft only if you already live in another.', reads awkwardly.

Do instead. Put the member's name first in every block. Shade hours outside the weekly schedule. Add a Day / Week / List switch and two header actions: 'Block time' and 'Edit weekly hours'. Use the right rail for the selected session (member, service, status, Join, Open member) or for 'Up next'. Move the calendar subscription to Connected calendars and rename it 'See your Eleva sessions in your own calendar app'.

What is weak. The mobile agenda lists only days that have bookings. The capture was taken on Saturday 14 and the first thing shown is Friday 13; today is absent, so the screen cannot answer 'am I free today?'. There is no week strip to tap a day, no dots showing which days have sessions, and rows have a chevron but no Join. The subscription card then takes a third of the screen. This is the screen an expert checks between sessions.

Do instead. Add a seven-day strip under the date range with today selected by default and a dot on days with sessions. Always render today, with 'Nothing booked today' and the next session when empty. Keep the agenda rows, add the member's name and an inline Join on the active online session. What is weak. Each row gives its second line to the URL path in monospace ('/fisiomota/follow-up'), then '3 delivery modes' as a count rather than naming them. P2XDASH-09uxService editor: six opaque tabs, and they break on mobileD5.4

What is weak. The editor has six horizontal tabs: Basics, Details, Kind, Policies, Delivery modes, Private links. 'Basics' versus 'Details' and 'Kind' do not tell an expert what is inside. Basics contains a 'Session mode' select while a separate 'Delivery modes' tab exists. Language tabs are nested inside the first tab. Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 20

08-marketing · Marketing and brand

Marketing pages: become an expert, for clinics, about

All three pages are tidy and honest, but the two pages for professionals describe the platform in careful, contract-like language and never show the product, a price block or a peer. The clinics page tells the reader three times that terms come later while asking her to create an account. The change that matters most: rebuild /become-expert around the offer an expert cares about (15% per booking and nothing else, your prices and policies, paid through Stripe), shown with real screens and a worked example.

  • The fee and payout timing are stated in exact figures on the page (15% of each booking, no other deductions, 7 days after payment or 24 hours after the session). That honesty is rare and worth making louder.

Findings

P1MKT-01copyThe /become-expert hero describes the platform; it does not make an offerD3.3

What is weak. The headline is 'Practise on Eleva.care' and the lead is a five-line paragraph: 'Eleva.care is a digital health platform for independent, licensed professionals. You keep full clinical autonomy. Eleva runs the scheduling, booking and payment technology...'. It reads like the first clause of an agreement. An expert with ten seconds does not learn what she gains, what it costs or how fast she can start. The homepage band that links here ('Grow your practice with Eleva. Bookings, payments and video sessions in one place, so you can focus on care') is a better pitch than the page itself. On mobile the paragraph runs to eight lines before the button.

Do instead. Lead with the outcome and three facts. Headline along the lines of 'Your practice, booked and paid in one place'. One line of lead. Then three short proof points under the button: '15% per booking, no monthly fee', 'You set your prices and cancellation policy', 'Paid to your bank through Stripe'. Primary button 'Create your account', secondary 'See how it works'. Move the clinical-independence sentence into the benefits below.

P1MKT-02uxThe fee is the strongest selling point and it is buried inside a paragraphD3.3

What is weak. 'Eleva keeps 15% of each booking, with no other deductions' appears in the middle of a 60-word card called 'Your rates and policies', and again inside step 01. There is no pricing block, no example of what an expert takes home, and payout timing is given as a rule ('the later of 7 days after payment or 24 hours after the session; Stripe then pays it to your bank') that needs reading twice. Price is the first thing a professional looks for; she has to hunt for it.

Do instead. Add a pricing section right after the benefits: '15% per booking. Nothing else.' as the heading, a checklist of what that includes (booking page, calendar, video sessions, reminders, payments), and a worked example ('A member pays 60 euros. You receive 51 euros.') or a small slider where the expert sets her session price. State payout timing as a short timeline: member pays, session happens, money reaches Stripe, Stripe pays your bank. Use only the figures already on the page and have finance confirm the example.

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 16

09-trust · Trust, legal and governance

Trust, legal and governance (cross-cutting)

The legal substance is unusually complete for a pre-launch product: consents are separate and unticked, every policy is dated, the controller is named, and export and deletion are in the product. The design does not yet let a member feel that. Trust facts sit in grey fine print, in documents and in FAQ accordions, while the moments that carry the most weight (the health-data consent, the pay step, the privacy controls) are the least explained. The one change that matters most: explain each trust moment in one plain sentence at the place where it is asked, starting with the health-data consent and the cancellation deadline next to the Pay button. References 13 and 14 (2026-11-21) prepare planned maintenance: a notice in advance with the exact window, and a status page that answers in one line. References 15 to 17 (2026-11-22) prepare the dashboard error page (slice 13.2): the error stays inside the app, 'Try again' works, there is a second way out and a reference to copy for support. References 18 to 33 (2026-11-23) prepare the trust centre and policy layout (slice D6.1) and the trust moments of the public site: the plain-language layer and contents on phones, acting on a right from the page that describes it, the cookie dialog, newsletter consent, who runs Eleva in the footer and on the contact page, the pay step and the accessibility statement.

Trust
Legal privacy

Keep

  • Checkout consents are four separate, unticked checkboxes, and the AI and transcription choice is marked Optional and left off (04-booking-checkout/05-paid-step-details). Keep the separation; improve the explanation.
  • The details step turns the cancellation policy into dated facts for this booking: "Full refund if you cancel before 15 Nov 2026, 10:00" (04-booking-checkout/06-paid-details-filled). This is the best trust line in the funnel.
  • Every card on the trust index has a one-line plain description and a last-updated date, and the page ends with privacy@ and security@ contacts plus a vulnerability disclosure page (09-trust/01-trust).
  • The privacy notice has a last-updated date, numbered sections, a sticky contents list on desktop, a purposes and legal bases table, the controller's legal name, NIPC and address, and the route to complain to the CNPD (09-trust/02-legal-privacy).
  • Consents, data export and account deletion live on one Privacy page in the member sidebar, deletion has a 14-day waiting period, and marketing notifications are off by default (10-member-space/05-privacy, 10-member-space/06-settings).
  • The "Need urgent help?" block with 112, SNS 24 and the crisis lines appears where a health note is typed and again on the thank-you page (04-booking-checkout/09-free-thank-you). It reads as care, not as a disclaimer.
  • The product already says who provides care: the hero line "Eleva connects you with independent health experts who run their own practice", the profile questions "Who provides my care?" and "What does Eleva check?", and the registration-check line on the experts page.
  • The profile shows the professional body, licence number and ERS registration number, and the footer links the electronic complaints book and reopens cookie settings.

Findings

P1TRUST-01trustThe health-data consent is a bare link at the moment it is askedD1.3

What is weak. The most sensitive choice in the product reads "I consent to health data processing", one of four identical grey rows under the heading "Policy and consent" and the intro "To book a health session on this digital health platform, please confirm:". Nothing on the screen says what health data means here, who sees it, or that the member can withdraw. The member has to leave a filled form and read a policy to find out. A woman booking pelvic health or fertility care wants that answer before she ticks. Consent that is given without understanding is also weaker consent: whether the label alone is specific and informed enough needs legal review. The note field "Anything you want the expert to know" sits a full card above the consent it depends on.

Do instead. Keep four separate unticked boxes. Rename the card "Before you book" and open it with a short promise in Lora, for example "Your health details stay between you and your expert", followed by two plain lines: who sees what you write (the expert you book), and that you can withdraw in Privacy settings. Give each checkbox a bold short label and one grey line of explanation: "Health information. I agree that Eleva handles the health details in this booking so my expert can prepare. Read the health data notice." Open each notice in a sheet or dialog so the form is never lost. Move the consent card directly under the note field on mobile so cause and consent are read together. Final wording needs legal review.

Judging criteria

The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 18

10-member-space · Dashboards

Member Space

The member Space is tidy and on brand, and its privacy controls are complete, but on first run it reads as an empty admin panel: home, sessions, reports, payments and inbox are each a dashed box saying nothing is here yet. Nothing welcomes a new member, helps her choose an expert, or explains how a session works. The one change that matters most is to turn home into a companion page: a next-session card with her expert, Join and what to prepare when something is booked, and a guided way to find the right expert when nothing is.

3 P111 P22 P317 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

Sessions

Payments
Privacy

Notifications

Session detail upcoming
Session detail past
Delete account confirm
Waiting room
Home video session
Payments paid
Session detail video

Keep

  • The visual language is calm and consistent with the rest of Eleva: Lora headings, generous cards, one teal primary action per block.
  • Every empty state on home and Sessions offers 'Find an expert', so there is always a way forward.
  • Privacy is complete and honest: consents, data download and account deletion are on one page, and deletion explains the 14-day waiting period and that it can be cancelled.
  • The join rule is already written in plain words in the product copy ('You can join video sessions from 15 minutes before the start. Sessions are not recorded.'); it deserves a more prominent place.
  • Settings covers what a member needs in one place: name, time zone, language, theme, notification channels and quiet hours.
  • The sidebar is short (six items) and uses words a member understands: Sessions, Payments, Reports, Privacy.

Findings

P1MEM-01uxFirst-run home is an empty admin panel, not a welcomeD5.2

What is weak. A new member sees 'Welcome, Demo', a subtitle that lists admin nouns ('Your sessions, payments, and privacy settings live in this Space') and two dashed boxes: 'You have no upcoming sessions.' and 'You have no past sessions yet.' The second box tells someone who has just arrived, a second time, that there is nothing here. 'Find an expert' appears twice within one screen and both send her away to the public directory with no guidance. Nothing explains what Eleva will do for her or how a session works. For a woman who may be anxious about a health concern, this is the first private page she sees, and it feels like a filing cabinet.

Do instead. Design a first-run home with one job: help her take the first step. Greeting by first name with a warm line ('Let's find the right expert for you'). A search field and need-based shortcuts in her words (Pregnancy, After birth, Pelvic floor, Breastfeeding, Nutrition, Emotional wellbeing) that open the directory already filtered. Two or three suggested experts with photo, speciality and next available time. A three-step 'How a session works' strip: book a time, get your link by email, join from here or from the email. Do not show 'Past sessions' until one exists.

Evidence:

Mobbin references: 10-member-space/0210-member-space/0410-member-space/03

P1MEM-02trustConsents page uses one 'Grant' button for everything and shows no stateD5.3

What is weak. Terms of use, Privacy notice, Health data processing, Marketing messages and AI help with session reports are listed the same way, each with a teal 'Grant' button and 'Version 2026-11-14'. Documents a member must accept to use Eleva look identical to optional choices, and the page does not show in words whether each is on or off. 'Grant' is legal language. On mobile this becomes five full-width primary buttons in a row. Only the AI item links to its text; the others cannot be read from here. The AI paragraph is seven lines of dense copy. On a health product, this is the page where a member decides whether she trusts Eleva with her data.

Do instead. Split into two blocks. 'What you agreed to': Terms of use, Privacy notice and Health data processing, each with 'Accepted on 14 Nov 2026', a 'Read' link, and no button (with a quiet 'Withdraw' link only where the law allows it and a sentence on what happens next). 'Your choices': Marketing messages and AI help with session reports as switches that show On or Off, each with one line on what changes. Rewrite the AI text as three short points: what it does, who sees it, how to turn it off. Replace 'Version 2026-11-14' with 'Updated 14 Nov 2026'.

P2MEM-03uxThe booked-session home could not be judged; define it as the page's main momentD0.1

What is weak. The demo member has no bookings, so the captures show only empty states. The source (apps/app/src/app/[orgSlug]/page.tsx) renders a featured booking card with a Join action and one small grey line about the 15-minute join window. That moment, the day before or the hour before a session, is when a member most needs reassurance: who she is meeting, when in her own time zone, how to join, and what to prepare. It should be captured with seeded data and reviewed against the references before the redesign is called done.

Do instead. Make the next session the hero of home: expert photo, name and speciality; service; date and time with time zone; mode; a countdown; a Join session button that is always visible and shows when it opens ('Opens at 09:45'); Add to calendar; Reschedule and Cancel with the cancellation policy summarised in one line. Under it, 'Before your session': fill in your intake notes, test your camera and microphone, find a quiet place. After the session, the same card becomes 'Your report from Ana is ready' or 'Book your follow-up'.

P2MEM-04uxSessions repeats home with two more empty boxesD5.2

What is weak. Sessions shows the same Upcoming and Past sections as home, with the same icons and nearly the same words, so two of six nav items lead to the same nothing. The empty heading packs two thoughts into one serif line ('No upcoming sessions. Find an expert to book your next visit.'). The subtitle, 'Review upcoming and past sessions with Eleva experts', describes the page rather than helping. The session detail page was not captured and could not be judged.

Do instead. Use one list with Upcoming and Past tabs, so only one empty state shows at a time. Each session row: expert photo and name, service, date tile, mode, status in words and the right action for its state (Join, Add to calendar, View report, Book again). The detail page should lead with the date in the title, then who, what and where, the join button with its opening time, and Reschedule and Cancel as clear but secondary actions.

P2MEM-05uxEmpty states are thin and inconsistentD5.2

What is weak. Payments says only 'No payments yet.' with no explanation of what will appear or why she would come back. Reports explains itself but offers no next step. Inbox is a single grey line, 'No notifications yet', with no card, icon or action, so it looks like a page that failed to load. Headings differ in punctuation and voice ('You have no upcoming sessions.', 'No reports yet', 'No payments yet.'). Each page fills less than a third of the screen and leaves the rest blank.

Do instead. Use one empty-state pattern everywhere: what will appear here, when, and one action. Payments: 'Your receipts will appear here after you book. You can download each one for your records.' Reports: 'After a session, your expert may share a written summary with you. We will email you when it is ready.' Inbox: 'You are all caught up. Booking updates and messages about your sessions arrive here.' Give each a relevant action (Find an expert, or Notification settings on Inbox). When Payments has data, each row should open a receipt with a clear breakdown and an 'Email receipt' action.

P2MEM-06uxNavigation: unlabeled 'Back', a hidden Inbox and no mobile barD5.2

What is weak. The sidebar starts with '← Back' and no destination, and nothing names the Space or the member, so she cannot tell where she is or where Back goes. The Inbox page is reached only from the bell, is titled 'Inbox' while the bell suggests notifications, and the sidebar highlights Home while she is on it. Reports, the most personal content, sits below Payments. There is no link to find an expert or get help. On mobile all six destinations are behind one icon, although a member mostly needs two: her next session and her reports.

Do instead. Replace Back with the Space name ('Demo's Space') and a labelled link such as 'Back to Eleva' or 'Find an expert'. Order the nav by care, then admin: Home, Sessions, Reports, Payments, then Settings and Privacy grouped under Account. Give Inbox its own active state and call the page 'Notifications' or the bell 'Inbox', not both. On mobile add a bottom bar: Home, Sessions, Reports, Account, with a badge on Sessions when one is coming up. Add Help at the bottom of the sidebar.

P2MEM-07a11yNotification settings lose a column on mobile and are hard to tapD5.5

What is weak. On desktop the notification grid has Email, SMS and In-app columns. On mobile only Email and SMS are visible and the capture is wider than the 390 px screen, so the page scrolls sideways and the third column is cut off. The grid uses small checkboxes with wide gaps on desktop and tight targets on mobile. Essential messages (session confirmations, reminders) can apparently be switched off entirely like marketing, with no sign of which are needed to attend a session. SMS can be ticked but the profile has no phone number field.

P2MEM-08copyData download and account deletion read like a policy, with no statusD5.3

What is weak. The deletion text uses internal terms: 'Account-scope data is erased', 'Booking-scope consents — the ones that authorised a session — are de-identified', 'retain-then-destroy rule', 'This cannot be shortened from this screen'. A member has to read it twice to learn what happens to her session notes. 'Request export' gives no sign of how long it takes, how she will be told, or whether an earlier request is still being prepared. The page subtitle, 'Consents, data export, and account deletion for this Space', is a list of features.

Do instead. Rewrite deletion as two short lists, 'What we erase' and 'What we keep, and why', in second person: 'We keep the record of your sessions for the time Portuguese law requires, with your name removed, and then destroy it.' Keep the 14-day waiting period and the cancel option as the last line before the button. For download, say 'We will email you a link when your file is ready. The link works for 24 hours.' and show a small history: requested on, status, download. New subtitle: 'See what you agreed to, get a copy of your data, or close your account.'

Click the photo to upload a custom image from your files.', 'Optional. Both start and end are required when enabled.', a raw 'Europe/Lisbon' time zone, and 'Manage your member profile, language, theme, and notifications.' Photo: 'Add a photo so your expert recognises you. Tap to choose one.' Quiet hours: 'Pause non-urgent messages at night. Choose a start and end time.' Show the time zone as 'Lisbon (GMT+0)'. Settings subtitle: 'Your name, language and how we reach you.'

    12-account-settings · Dashboards

    Account settings

    A person had two settings pages and two privacy pages. /space/settings and /account/settings both edited the same photo, name and language on the user record, but each held only some controls: time zone, theme and notifications were only in the Space, and password, two-step verification, passkeys and devices only in /account. /account/privacy was a signpost to /space/privacy. The fix is one home for everything about the person, /account, in short pages (Profile, Notifications, Security, Privacy, Workspaces, Billing for practices), with a strict hierarchy: one headline and one line per page, one title and one line per card, a hint only where it prevents a mistake or says who sees a value, and background explanation in an (i) popover.

    3 P14 P20 P312 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

    Captures

    Profile
    Notifications
    Security
    Security with password
    Privacy
    Billing
    Workspaces
    Old space settings
    Old space privacy
    Notifications help
    Delete account confirm
    Two step scan
    Two step code
    Two step backup codes
    Consent details

    Keep

    • The cards, Lora headings and one teal action per block are calm and on brand; the merge keeps them.
    • Every control already went through apps/api (/me, /users, /privacy) with Zod and audit, so moving the pages needs no API change.
    • Privacy was complete: consents, a data copy with status, and deletion with a 14-day waiting period that can be cancelled.
    • Passkeys, two-step verification and Google linking were already wired to Better Auth.

    Findings

    P1ACC-01uxTwo settings pages and two privacy pages for the same personD5.8

    What is weak. /space/settings and /account/settings both edit the photo, name and language stored on the user, with different wording for the same card. Time zone, theme and notifications exist only in the Space; password, two-step verification, passkeys, Google and devices only in /account. /account/privacy only describes three controls and links to /space/privacy. A member cannot tell which page is the real one, and asks whether she must set things up twice.

    Do instead. One home for everything about the person: /account. Pages: Profile (photo, name, email, language, time zone, appearance), Notifications, Security, Privacy, Workspaces, and Billing only for practices and clinics. /space/settings and /space/privacy redirect there, and the Space sidebar keeps Settings and Privacy under an 'Account' group that opens /account.

    Evidence:

    Mobbin references: 12-account-settings/0212-account-settings/03

    P1ACC-02trustNotification switches promise choices Eleva does not honourD5.8

    What is weak. The grid lets a member untick Payments and System, but those messages are always sent (REQUIRED_NOTIFICATION_CATEGORIES). It offers SMS and quiet hours, but texts need a verified phone number that nothing collects, and quiet hours only apply to texts. The Marketing row changes nothing: news emails follow the marketing consent on the Privacy page. A member can turn off session emails, which carry her join link.

    Do instead. Show only real choices. Sessions and reminders: email and in-app switches that save at once (the backend honours them). Payments and Account and security: switches that are on and locked, marked 'Always on'. Point news from Eleva to the Privacy page. Bring back text messages and quiet hours together with adding and verifying a mobile number.

    Evidence:

    Mobbin references: 12-account-settings/0110-member-space/10

    P1ACC-03trustSign-up does not record Terms and Privacy acceptanceD5.3

    What is weak. Consents are written by the booking funnel and guest activation only. A person who signs up and has not booked has no Terms or Privacy row, so the old page showed 'Grant' next to Terms of use and Privacy notice for a signed-up member. The new page shows 'Updated {date}' with a Read link in that case, but the record itself is missing.

    Do instead. Record terms and privacy (current CONSENT_DOCUMENT_VERSION) when the account is created, from the sign-up screen's agreement, through @eleva/compliance with audit. Then 'What you agreed to' shows 'Agreed on {date}' for everyone. Needs legal review of the sign-up wording.

    Evidence:

    Mobbin references: 10-member-space/08

    P2ACC-04uxSecurity mixed into profile, with raw device strings and a hidden 2FA stepD5.8

    What is weak. Password, two-factor, passkeys, Google and sessions are one card under the profile. The password form shows to people who sign in with Google or an email link. 'Enable authenticator' silently uses the current-password field and prints a raw otpauth URI. Sessions list 29 'Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0…' strings with 'Revoke', no 'this device' and no way to sign out of all others.

    Do instead. A Security page: Password (or one line saying none is needed), Two-step verification as a short dialog (password, setup key with copy and an app link, backup codes, code), Passkeys with a list and an empty state, Google, and 'Where you're signed in' with 'Chrome on macOS', 'This device', last active, 'Sign out' and 'Sign out of all other devices'.

    Evidence:

    Mobbin references: 12-account-settings/0112-account-settings/0512-account-settings/0612-account-settings/0912-account-settings/10

    P2ACC-05copyNo hierarchy between headline, title, hint and helpD5.8

    What is weak. Every page repeats an 'ACCOUNT' eyebrow the sidebar already shows. Footers repeat the title or say things that are not true or not useful ('Email and identity changes may require verification', 'These preferences are used when we start sending notifications', 'Optional. Both start and end are required when enabled.'). The photo relies on 'Click the photo'. Long legal text sits on the page while short help has nowhere to go. The language select overlaps its title on phones.

    Do instead. Headline and one line per page, no eyebrow. Card: title and one line on why it matters. Field: label, and a hint only when it prevents a mistake or says who sees the value. Footer: state or consequence, then the action. Background in an (i) popover with an accessible name. What a member must know before an irreversible step goes in the confirm dialog.

    Evidence:

    Mobbin references: 12-account-settings/0312-account-settings/0412-account-settings/0712-account-settings/08

    P2ACC-06uxBilling offers expert and clinic plans to membersD5.8

    What is weak. A member with no practice sees Expert Community, Top Expert (pre-selected), Clinic Starter and Clinic Growth, and 'Start an embedded Stripe Checkout session'. Plan names and descriptions are hard-coded in English.

    Do instead. Show Billing only to people with an expert practice or a clinic; a member who opens the address sees that receipts live in her Space with a link to Payments. Plan copy, translations and moving plans into practice settings follow in the expert consistency pass.

    Evidence:

    P2ACC-07copyConsent switches carry the whole notice inlineD5.9

    What is weak. Health data, news and AI each showed long paragraphs and a bullet list under the switch, so the Privacy page read as a legal wall.

    Do instead. Layered notice: each row shows the purpose, what it covers and what turning it on means in one line (health data names 'health information' and who uses it); a 'Details' dialog holds the bullets and the link to the full notice. News needs no Details.

      14-content-pages · UX writing and content

      Content pages: newsletter, podcast, community, evidence, contact, history

      These six pages have no captures yet, so this surface holds references and judging criteria only. Today /newsletter, /podcast and /community are a name, one paragraph of 17 or 18 words and one button each; they name the vendor but not what arrives, how often, or what an issue or episode is like. /contact names four routes in plain words but gives no reply time, /evidence-based-care opens with a definition and reads like a policy, and the founder's letter on /history runs to 619 words under headings that are partly labels. The references show how shipped sites say these things in few words: a promise with its rhythm, an episode with its length, a reply time, a letter that starts with the reader.

        Judging criteria

        The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 8

        15-brand-art-direction · Brand and art direction

        Brand and art direction for the public site

        The public site is tidy, honest and calm, and it could belong to anyone. Deep teal does every job, the photographs come from many shoots with no shared treatment, the serif never gets large enough to show character, and every section is the same row of rounded cards. The references here show how health and wellness brands build a recognisable identity from a few decisions made firmly: a palette with a role for each colour, one photographic treatment, one display moment per page, a small set of shapes, and a signature ending. Three worked directions with palettes, type and contrast figures are in the panel's brand-directions.md. The change that matters most, whichever direction is chosen: give each colour one job and put every photograph through one treatment.

        3 P13 P21 P326 Mobbin referencesAfter captured

        Captures

        Tide home
        Clay home
        Folio home
        Tide profile pay
        Clay profile pay
        Folio profile pay
        Estuary home
        Estuary profile pay
        Tide first screen

        Keep

        • Cream paper with deep teal already reads calm and trustworthy, and text contrast is strong: ink on the page is 16 to 1, teal on the page 5.8 to 1 and the button label 5.7 to 1, by calculation.
        • Fraunces with DM Sans is a sound pair, already self-hosted, and the tokens hold fluid display steps and warm shadows that a new direction can reuse.
        • The large rounded portrait on the expert profile is the most distinctive picture on the site, and the deep teal quote band shows that one strong field works.
        • The leaf mark and wordmark are recognisable, and the mono eyebrow gives pages a quiet structure worth keeping.

        Findings

        P1BRAND-01uiOne colour does every job, so nothing stands outD8.1

        What is weak. Deep teal (#006D77) is the header button, every link, the numerals, the icon discs, the chip text, the eyebrow and the two dark bands. Coral appears once on the homepage, as the 'Become an expert' button, and nowhere on /become-expert. The tokens hold a full coral scale, a sand scale and three highlight colours, but no colour has a stated role on the public site. With the logo covered, the page could belong to any careful health or finance brand.

        Do instead. Write a palette of five to seven colours with one job each: page, surface, text, action, emphasis words, one deep field, and one tint that only ever marks trust or health facts ('Registration checked', a session time). Use the action colour on nothing that cannot be pressed. Three worked palettes with contrast figures are in brand-directions.md.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0315-brand-art-direction/0415-brand-art-direction/0715-brand-art-direction/1815-brand-art-direction/1915-brand-art-direction/22

        P1BRAND-02uiThe photographs do not look like one brandD8.1

        What is weak. The homepage hero is a dark collage of three stock pictures. The four service tiles come from four shoots with four kinds of light. The advisors on About stand in front of grey studio paper, a white wall, a red wall, a garden and a conference stage, at different crops. The brand book already says 'mixed lighting styles in one page without intent' is a don't, and asks for one headshot spec that has not been written.

        Do instead. Choose one treatment and apply it to everything this month, before any shoot: cut-outs on brand tints, or black and white under one colour wash, at one crop. Then write a one-page photo guide for experts (open shade, chest up, plain wall) and commission about ten documentary photographs in real rooms for the marketing pages. Replace stock service tiles with type or shapes until real pictures exist.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0215-brand-art-direction/0515-brand-art-direction/0615-brand-art-direction/1015-brand-art-direction/1115-brand-art-direction/12

        P1BRAND-03uiThe serif has no moment of scale, and the italic is spent on every headingD8.1

        What is weak. At 1440px the hero headline is about 56px and section headings about 44 to 48px, by estimate, so the largest type is 4% of the viewport width. Fraunces at that size reads as a tidy serif and shows little of its character. Five of six homepage headings end in an italic phrase ('on your schedule', 'women's health', 'tailored to you', 'lifelong journey', 'with Eleva'), so the italic no longer signals anything. The brand book names Lora as the headline face while packages/ui/src/fonts.ts ships Fraunces; the two documents disagree.

        Do instead. Give each page one display moment at 8 to 10% of the viewport width on desktop and 12 to 14% on a phone, and keep other headings modest. Reserve italic (or the accent colour) for one phrase per page. Decide the display face on purpose and correct the brand book to match the code.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0115-brand-art-direction/0415-brand-art-direction/1315-brand-art-direction/1415-brand-art-direction/20

        P2BRAND-04uiThere is no shape or illustration languageD8.1

        What is weak. The only graphic devices are a rounded rectangle and a small teal disc behind an icon. The leaf in the logo, which the brand book calls the motif, is not used anywhere else. Pages without photographs (the benefits grid on /become-expert, 'What we stand for' on About) fall back to icon-in-disc cards, the most common pattern on the web.

        Do instead. Draw four or five shapes from the mark (leaf, arch, disc, half disc) and use them three ways: as a frame for portraits, as a large cropped field in closing sections, and in place of stock pictures where no real photograph exists. Keep to two or three colours per composition.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0915-brand-art-direction/1615-brand-art-direction/2315-brand-art-direction/05

        P2BRAND-05uiEvery section is the same block: eyebrow, serif heading, paragraph, a row of rounded cardsD8.1

        What is weak. The homepage repeats one template seven times and About repeats it eight times. Columns are equal, pictures are the same size within a row and every block is centred on the same width. There is no lead item, no numbered sequence with lines, no text set in two columns and no picture that breaks the grid. The page is easy to scan but has no rhythm, and nothing tells the reader which part matters most.

        Do instead. Alternate three or four layouts: one lead with four smaller items; numbered rows on hairlines; a statement with a two-column story; one tall picture beside a short text. Allow one picture per page to bleed off an edge. Keep cards for things that are objects (an expert, a service).

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/1515-brand-art-direction/1615-brand-art-direction/1715-brand-art-direction/1315-brand-art-direction/01

        P2BRAND-06uiThe page and its surfaces are almost the same colour, and the deep band is used twiceD8.1

        What is weak. The page is sand-50 (#FDFAF5), the alternate sections are sand-100 (#F9F3EB) and the cards are white. The three differ by a few points of lightness, so on most screens the sections run together and the 'cream' reads as off-white. The one strong field, deep teal, appears twice on the homepage (the quote and the expert call to action), which halves its effect.

        Do instead. Deepen the page colour until it is clearly warm next to a white card, and give alternate sections a real second colour. Use the deep field once per page for the single most important statement, with type large enough to deserve it.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0115-brand-art-direction/0315-brand-art-direction/1915-brand-art-direction/2015-brand-art-direction/21

        P3BRAND-07uiPages end without a signatureD8.1

        What is weak. The footer is a small logo and three columns of links on the same cream as the page, with nineteen links at one size. The closing section above it is a different pattern on each page (a teal photo block on the homepage, a plain heading and button on /become-expert, nothing on the profile). The last screen of every page is the least branded.

        Do instead. Give every page the same ending: a closing block with one brand shape or the deep colour, one sentence and one action, then a footer where the wordmark or leaf appears large and the legal links sit small beneath.

        Evidence:

        Mobbin references: 15-brand-art-direction/0815-brand-art-direction/2315-brand-art-direction/24

The lead image is a collage of capsules on green discs over a pale grid, so even the picture uses shapes.

        Eleva takes: A hierarchy of one and four reads as a magazine, where four equal cards read as a catalogue. Eleva can use it for the evidence and guide pages and for 'How we support you' (one lead need, four others). The mono tag is already in Eleva's system as the eyebrow.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/17 Zaro web · section

        Numbered rows divided by hairlines, with the open row in ink and the rest in grey

        On off-white (#FAFAF8), the heading is a 32px medium sans whose second clause turns warm grey-brown. Three rows numbered 01, 02 and 03 are separated by 1px lines. The open row is ink at 26px with one line of explanation; the closed rows are grey. A soft, blurred warm photograph on the right carries two white chips. No card has a border or a fill.

        Eleva takes: Eleva's 'How it works' already has 01, 02, 03 in teal italic numerals. Hairlines and one open row would turn it from three equal blocks into a sequence, and would work the same on a phone. A data product; kept for the structure.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/18 Ragged Edge web · section

        Three colour blocks with a role each, and two type voices

        On a pale blush page (#FBF7F6), a charcoal block (#1F1F1D) carries five stacked words in blush bold geometric sans at about 96px, with a short serif line in the corner. Under it, an olive block (about #768437) holds a 30px serif sentence about one customer, and a blush block (#F8EDE6) holds the call to action in bold sans. The bright pink appears only in the logo. Sans speaks for the brand and serif speaks for people.

        Eleva takes: A palette of three fields used with intent: the dark one for the brand statement, the mid one for a human story, the light one for the action. Eleva could give its deep colour, a warm mid colour and a tint the same three roles, and keep serif for human voices (quotes, experts' words) and sans for facts. An agency case study for an insurer; kept for the colour and type logic.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/19 Klarna web · section

        A full-width mauve section with plum-black type

        The section is one flat mauve (#B698BC) from edge to edge. The heading is a condensed bold sans at about 32px in plum-black (#24202C), and four figures at 30px sit in a row with 12px labels. Everything is left-aligned with a margin of about an eighth of the width. There are no cards, lines or icons.

        Eleva takes: A coloured section needs no cards inside it. Mauve with plum-black is calm, clearly not clinical blue or green, and passes contrast with room to spare (about 6.2 to 1 by calculation). It is evidence for a departure from teal. A payments company; kept for the colour pair.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/20 Craft Agency web · section

        Deep green ground, ivory serif capitals, one line roman and one italic

        The ground is a deep green close to black (#17271C). Two lines of high-contrast serif capitals in ivory (about #EDE8DC) run at roughly 10% of the viewport width: the first roman and left-aligned, the second italic and pushed right until it leaves the screen. A soft green and lilac gradient shape glows behind. The body is three lines of 14px ivory text set low and left.

        Eleva takes: A deep ground with ivory serif is premium and calm at once, and roman against italic gives contrast without a second colour. Eleva's deep band could use this once per page with type three times today's size. Capitals at this size suit two or three words only. A talent consultancy; kept for the type and colour.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/21 Frontify web · section

        A serif pull quote on a dark band, set like a page in a magazine

        On near-black (#11110F), the speaker's company sits alone in a narrow left column. The quote runs in a light serif at about 30px, four lines of about 40 characters, starting a third of the way in. The attribution is 11px beneath, and 'Read story' with an arrow sits at the far right on the same baseline. No quotation-mark graphic, no portrait, no card.

        Eleva takes: Eleva's quote band centres a long quote with a small avatar. Setting it on a grid (who on the left, words on the right, one link) makes it read as editorial. It also shows restraint: the dark band is used once. Eleva uses its deep teal band twice on the homepage. A brand-management tool; kept for the layout.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/22 Monarch web · section

        One shape language: pills for actions, 12px for panels, one accent only on what you can press

        A warm grey panel (#EDECEA) with a 12px radius sits on an off-white page (#F9F9F7). The heading is a centred serif at about 44px. Of four feature blocks, the active one is a white card with the same 12px radius; the others fade to half strength. Orange (about #F9772B) appears only on the 13px uppercase labels and on pill buttons 44px tall; 'Sign in' is a white pill with a hairline.

        Eleva takes: Two radii, used without exception: full pills for anything pressable, 12px for anything that holds content. The accent marks only actions and labels. Eleva can adopt the same rule with its own values. Do not take the colour pair: white on this orange is about 2.7 to 1 by calculation, under the 4.5 to 1 Eleva needs. A budgeting app; kept for the shape rules.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/23 metic. web · section

        A closing card with one large shape, one sentence and one action

        A charcoal card (#131315) with an 8px radius sits on a pale grey page. A single red disc (#FF3038), about 40% of the card's width, is cropped by the top-right corner. The heading is white sans at about 48px over three short lines; the body is grey at 18px, about 22 characters a line; the one action is an outlined pill with a red circular arrow.

        Eleva takes: A closing section does not need a photograph. One brand shape cropped large, one plain sentence and one action would end Eleva's pages with more character than the current photo-and-teal block, and it costs nothing to produce. Eleva's shape would be the leaf or an arch in its accent colour. A design studio; kept for the composition.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/24 Structured web · section

        The footer is the wordmark, set as wide as the screen

        On light grey (#EBEBEB), the name is set in a black high-contrast serif that spans about 96% of the viewport width, with a cap height near 17% of the width. Six links sit in 9px capitals at the top right and three legal links in a row beneath the name. That is the whole footer.

        Eleva takes: The last thing a visitor sees is the name, large. Eleva keeps its logo, so the equivalent is the existing wordmark and leaf at full width in a tone close to the ground (deep on deep, or sand on sand), with the link columns above it. It gives the brand a signature on every page without a new asset. A finance protocol; kept for the footer idea.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/25 Waabi web · section

        A film fills the first screen and a short headline sits over its lower left

        The whole screen is one moving picture. The headline is two short sentences in a serif at an ordinary size, set over the quiet part of the frame, and the navigation is a small bar at the top. Nothing else is on the screen, so the picture carries the character and the words stay easy to read.

        Eleva takes: Eleva's hero as the film with one question over its lower left and one action under it. The headline does not need to be large when the picture is doing the work. A self-driving truck company; kept for the composition only.

        Open on Mobbin

        15-brand-art-direction/26 Superpower web · section

        A hero inside a rounded frame: one person, one colour of light, a headline and its action on the left

        The picture sits in a frame with rounded corners and a small margin, so it reads as an object on the page and not a banner. One woman in profile, lit by one warm colour. The headline, one line and the main button share the left edge, and three short facts sit along the bottom. The colour comes from the light in the photograph, not from a gradient laid over it.

        Eleva takes: Keep Eleva's film in a rounded frame with a small margin, and let colour come from the footage and from two flat fields lower on the page (teal and coral). A health-testing company in the US; its eligibility line is specific to that market and is not something Eleva shows. Kept for the frame and the light.

        Judging criteria

        The review panel scores the "after" captures against these, with the references above open. 0 / 8

        awwwards · Awwwards seat

        Awwwards reference library

        Twenty-three sites that the Awwwards jury recognised and that teach Eleva something about art direction or page structure: health and care brands, booking products, calm editorial sites, brand systems and two trust-heavy products. Awards, dates and scores are copied from each site's Awwwards page; an Honorable Mention page shows no scores, so those entries have none. The captures show each live site on 23 November 2026, which is not always the design the jury saw; where it has changed, the entry says so.

        23 award-winning sites

        awwwards/01 Heva Health health

        Site of the Day, 26 July 2024, and Developer Award (its page gives no date) · Overall 7.11: Design 7.18, Usability 7.04, Creativity 7.04, Content 7.25

        A two-colour brand carries a whole clinic: cream and deep olive, a light condensed serif with italics for headlines ("Vitality, refined.") and a small grotesque for body text, over warm dusk photography. The page then answers the three trust questions in order. "The people behind every protocol" shows four clinicians with portrait, credentials, focus tags and a short bio. "Three steps, one path forward" numbers the way in. The FAQ is written as real questions from named people ("Charles from New York asks: How much does Heva actually cost?").

        Eleva takes: Homepage: show four checked experts with portrait, title, focus tags and two lines of bio, before any testimonial. FAQ on the homepage and on become an expert: write each question the way a member would ask it. Brand as a whole: one pill-shaped navigation bar over the hero photo, and a palette of two colours plus photography.

        Not to copy: The hero and sections have changed since the award; the palette and type are the same. A 30% discount form interrupts the page after the hero, and the page uses before and after body photos; Eleva takes neither. The full capture is cropped above the footer, which carries a US compliance badge.

        Open the site · Open on Awwwards

        awwwards/02 Function Health health

        Honorable Mention, 9 July 2024

        The first screen is one portrait, a three-word serif headline ("Check your health.") and a strip of three facts with a label under each (160+ lab tests, whole body, $1 per day). Every section heading is a serif sentence with one word in terracotta italics ("Testing is easy", "Know what to do next"). Cream background, terracotta buttons, a grotesque for body text. A comparison table ("Not your average checkup") and a price card ("What could cost you $15,000 is $365") say the offer in numbers.

        Eleva takes: Homepage hero: a facts strip under the headline with three things Eleva can prove (experts checked, session length, starting price). Homepage: a short table of booking with Eleva against finding an expert alone. Brand as a whole: the heading pattern of one emphasised word in italics works with a serif such as Lora.

        Not to copy: The page is about 14,000px long and leans on celebrity quotes and press logos. The full capture shows the cookie panel over the hero. The medical board is shown far down the page; Eleva should show its experts early.

        Open the site · Open on Awwwards

        awwwards/03 Maxima Therapy health

        Site of the Day, 7 April 2026, and Developer Award (its page gives no date) · Overall 7.73: Design 7.80, Usability 7.38, Creativity 8.12, Content 7.76

        A therapy provider owns an illustration language instead of stock photos: flat shapes with small faces in yellow, orange-red, blue and green, a heavy condensed display face in capitals and a rounded grotesque for reading. The characters even sit on top of the one photograph. Near the end, a calm white card states the worry and answers it: "We understand this can be a big step, but we made the process as quick, easy, and stress-free as possible", with three named steps.

        Eleva takes: Brand as a whole: commission a small set of illustrations Eleva owns (people, bodies, life stages) so that pages without photography still look like Eleva. Homepage and become an expert: a reassurance card that names the worry, then three steps.

        Not to copy: The page is driven by scroll animation and has long empty stretches; the helper's full-page shot came out mostly blank and the capture here was taken one screen at a time. The primary colours and the playful tone suit children's services, not an adult health companion. Usability is its lowest jury score.

        Open the site · Open on Awwwards

        awwwards/04 Hello Period health

        Honorable Mention, 12 April 2024

        A women's health brand that is warm and direct without being clinical: a red-orange wordmark and headings in a high-contrast serif, on mint, blush, lilac and pale blue blocks, with products shot on flat colour. Trust is built in layers down the page: press logos, star reviews marked "Verified", a live counter ("804,726,717 single-use period products we've saved from the landfill") and a row of four facts with icons, among them that it was designed by a nurse and is female founded. "Hello Academy" gathers a comparison chart, a quiz and a how-to in three cards.

        Eleva takes: Homepage: a row of four plain facts about who is behind Eleva. Content pages: a three-card learning strip (a guide, a short quiz that points to the right kind of expert, a how-it-works). Brand as a whole: a pastel family used as section backgrounds with one strong accent for headings and buttons.

        Not to copy: It is a shop, so the hero is a product carousel and the page pushes bundles and discounts. The hero has changed since the award. Six background colours on one page is the upper limit; Eleva should use fewer.

        Open the site · Open on Awwwards

        awwwards/05 Q Psychology health

        Honorable Mention, 23 January 2025

        The team page is a small, calm directory: two rows of filter chips (clinic location, practice area), then portraits in arch-shaped frames with name, pronouns, role, location tags and a "See profile" button. The fees page puts every price in one place: an accordion per service with fee and rebate, a line for the cancellation policy and two questions about payment. The brand is deep green and mint on off-white, very large light serif headlines and photographs of the real rooms and the real team. The footer ends with a crisis line in its own strip.

        Eleva takes: Explorer: filter chips above the grid and a card that shows portrait, name, title, mode and place, with one button. Trust and legal: a single page for prices, what a refund depends on and how to cancel, as accordions. Site footer: a line that says where to go in an emergency.

        Not to copy: On desktop the hero sets white serif text over a busy photo and the paragraph is hard to read. The hero headline runs to four lines.

        Open the site · Open on Awwwards

        awwwards/06 Roczen health

        Honorable Mention, 27 January 2023

        A UK care programme shows its evidence in a fixed order. First, "Clinically proven results": four numbers, each with its unit and a one-line label. Then one plain sentence on who evaluated the service, with the journals named. Then reviews, each signed "Member". Then the organisations that use it, and the regulator's mark in the footer. The FAQ starts with "Who are my doctors and nurses?". It calls the people it serves members, as Eleva does.

        Eleva takes: Homepage and the evidence-based care page: an evidence band in this order (numbers Eleva can stand behind, who checks the experts, member words, where Eleva is registered). FAQ: open with who the experts are. About: name the controller and registration in the footer.

        Not to copy: The subject is weight management; the structure is the lesson. Sections fade in on scroll, so the helper's full-page shot was blank and the capture was taken one screen at a time. The pastel gradient and blue are generic.

        awwwards/07 Klearmind Clinics health

        Honorable Mention, 30 August 2025

        Imagery for a medical service that is neither stock photos nor cartoons: single flowers cut out on blush and cream, and one collage of a woman's face with flowers. White, blush and cream with orange buttons, a light soft serif for headlines and a plain sans for text. The structure is careful too: "A clear path from questions to care" as four cards, and "Know the risks before treatment" as a plain list beside a photo of a consultation, before any sales message.

        Eleva takes: Brand as a whole: botanical still life as a photography direction for pages where portraits are not right (trust, legal, empty states). Homepage: four step cards from first question to first session. Profile and checkout: say what a session cannot do, plainly, beside what it can.

        Not to copy: This is a ketamine clinic in California; take the art direction and the structure, nothing about the service. The full capture stops before the sections that are specific to US rules. The light headline weight gets thin on a phone.

        awwwards/08 Letters health

        Honorable Mention, 23 April 2025

        A page that sells a tool to clinicians in their own terms: "Patients, not paperwork", the saving in hours in the second line, and a before and after of the actual document under the button. "Your data is safe" is three tiles that each state one fact, the strongest being "Your data never leaves Australia" with the city named. Pricing is three cards with a free tier first. Sky-blue gradient, white cards, black pill buttons and a rounded grotesque.

        Eleva takes: Become an expert: lead with what the expert gets back (time, members, payouts), then show the real product, then three data tiles that state facts (where records are stored in the EU, who can read them, what is never stored). Clinics: the same tiles, plus pricing cards.

        Not to copy: It says "patients"; Eleva says members. "Bank-grade protection" is a vague claim; the tile that names the country is the one to copy. Headings animate on scroll and leave gaps in the capture.

        awwwards/09 Therapy in London marketplace

        Honorable Mention, 10 January 2025

        The closest match to Eleva in the library. The hero is the search itself, two questions in plain words: "What do you need help with?" and "Where are you based?". The profile lets the therapist speak: a quote, a welcome video, "I am going to help you by" as three step cards, then prices in a two-cell table ("Telephone Consultation (15 mins) Free", "Individual Session (50 minutes) £150"), tags for therapy types and session types, and the membership body with the registration number. The join page gives four steps, says which documents are checked and how long approval takes ("up to 72 hours"), and prints the cost on two stamps. Paper beige with blue, green, lilac and orange, ruled lines and hand-drawn furniture, a geometric grotesque.

        Eleva takes: Homepage hero: a need question and a place or mode question as the first thing on the page. Profile: a first free call and the session price side by side, a short "how I work" in three steps, and the professional body with the register number. Become an expert: steps, the documents Eleva checks, the review time and the cost, all on one page.

        Not to copy: Heavy scroll animation, tilted cards and words that draw themselves; the helper's full-page shot was blank and these captures were taken one screen at a time, so the profile's fixed side panel repeats down the image. The profile is very long. The personal prompts (favourite colour, what I am watching) are too casual for a clinical expert.

        awwwards/10 Contra marketplace

        Honorable Mention, 16 April 2024

The first shelf is "Verified studios", with a green mark beside the heading and beside each name. The footer is split by audience ("For independents", "For companies"). Black on white, one grotesque.

        awwwards/11 Hi, skin marketplace

        Site of the Day, 9 January 2021, and Developer Award (its page gives no date). Both were given to an earlier design; the live site has been redesigned since. · Overall 7.37: Design 7.59, Usability 7.16, Creativity 7.24, Content 7.37 (the 2021 design)

        A booking product puts proof beside the button: "185,000+ facials | 4.9 stars" above the headline and "4/5 members strongly recommend us" under it. One entry service is named with its price ("Starting at $119") and six outcomes. "How it works" is three words: Assess, Treat, Results. The first booking step is a single choice, "Select a location", sorted by distance with opening hours, and a bar fixed to the bottom that repeats the choice and holds the one "Next" button.

        Eleva takes: Checkout: one decision per step and a fixed bar that repeats what the member chose and carries the only primary button. Profile: lead with one named first session, its price and what it includes. Homepage hero: a line of proof directly above the headline.

        Not to copy: Not the design the jury scored; kept for the live booking flow. Capital-letter headlines, electric blue and before and after photos are not Eleva's voice. A discount form sits in the footer.

        awwwards/12 Core Atelier Pilates marketplace

        Honorable Mention, 25 March 2026

        A warm, premium palette that is not pink: blush and espresso brown, with one mid-brown band for the testimonial. Headlines are a large old-style serif in lower case, with the second half in italics ("elevated pilates, crafted for you."). The photographs show the room in daylight, with one person small in the frame. One member quote is shown at a time, counted ("1 of 5 reflections"), with first name and initial.

        Not to copy: The booking page opens with a "packages required" dialog over the class list before a visitor can look; Eleva lets people browse first. White text over the hero photo is low in contrast at the left edge.

        awwwards/13 Designed by Women editorial

        Site of the Day, 4 January 2021, and Developer Award (its page gives no date) · Overall 7.52: Design 7.56, Usability 7.37, Creativity 7.42, Content 8.02

        An editorial site about women's work with the highest Content score in this library (8.02). Each section has a small orange label (About, Exhibition, Designers, Work, Story), a bold soft serif headline and one short paragraph. The people are listed as a typographic index: a name per row with dates, ruled lines between, one "Discover" button. "Designer of the month" gives one person a full-width portrait.         awwwards/14 ORDR editorial

        Honorable Mention, 29 April 2026

        A health newsletter page in five short moves. The promise in three lines ("Clear, actionable wellness insights delivered in a 5-minute weekly newsletter. Completely Free."), the email field in the first screen, "New here? Check it out" with a sample issue, an archive as overlapping cards, and a second sign-up at the end. The small print under the field says "Completely free. Leave whenever." Paper white and charcoal green, a condensed serif in capitals, one grainy black and white photograph.

        awwwards/20 Twofold Therapy brand

        Honorable Mention, 2 August 2026

        A photographic idea that says what the service is without a caption: double exposures of one woman in two positions, in muted grey and beige. The type mixes a bold grotesque and a text serif inside one heading ("Individual psychotherapy / and psychoanalysis"). Services are a numbered table, 01 to 04, with the name in serif and two lines of description at the right. White, soft grey and black only.

        Eleva takes: Brand as a whole: commission one photographic idea for mental health and for change over time (pregnancy, recovery, menopause) instead of buying stock. Profile and offers: a numbered list of services with two lines each.

        Not to copy: There is no booking action in the first screens and no guidance for a nervous visitor. Paragraphs are set tight in a bold face and are tiring to read. It is quiet to the point of being cold.

        awwwards/21 Wise Design brand

        Site of the Day, 24 March 2023, and Developer Award (its page gives no date) · Overall 7.55: Design 7.69, Usability 7.50, Creativity 7.33, Content 7.52

        A money company that people must trust publishes its brand rules as a public site. "Direction" is a grid of tiles, one per part of the system: Brand, Cards, Colour, Flags, Icons, Illustration, Logo, Motion. The identity rests on one pair, bright green on forest green, with a grotesque. "Inspiration" shows the brand in use as a strip of photographs in pill and circle masks.

        Eleva takes: Brand as a whole: after the rethink, turn the brand book into a small public page with one tile per part (colour, type, photography, illustration, voice, motion), so experts, clinics and press use it correctly. A confident two-colour core is easier to trust and to keep consistent than a wide palette.

        Not to copy: The homepage is a single screen of moving images with no words, so it has no full-page capture and tells a newcomer nothing. The lesson is the system, not the page. Semantics and SEO is its lowest developer mark (6.40).

        awwwards/22 Butter Insurance trust

        Honorable Mention, 16 August 2024

        Insurance explained in amounts, not adjectives. Each cover is a tile with its limit as a small label ("Unlimited", "Up to $40,000") and one sentence in plain words ("We'll cover your pre-paid, non-refundable trip costs if you need to cancel or interrupt your trip."). "Total peace of mind" is a set of tiles that each hold one fact (24/7, $0 excess, 173 countries). Extras are switches. Every claim with a condition carries an asterisk that is answered in the footer, beside the company and licence details. The FAQ page opens with "The things travellers ask us most, explained without the jargon" and groups questions by moment: "Before you buy", "Your policy and portal", "What is and isn't covered", "Optional packs", "If something goes wrong".

        Eleva takes: Trust and legal: group the help and policy questions by moment (before you book, your booking, what a session includes, if something goes wrong) and open each legal page with one plain sentence on what it covers. Checkout: show what is included and the refund rule as amounts and times. Footer: name the controller and registration beside the small print.

        Not to copy: It opens with a loader of several seconds; the helper captured only the loader twice, and these captures needed a 12 second wait. Bright yellow and black is loud for health. The footer small print is very small.

        awwwards/23 Counter Culture Coffee, Transparency Report trust

        Honorable Mention, 18 July 2024, given to the 2023 edition. The same address now shows the 2025 edition, with new art direction.

        A company earns trust by publishing its own numbers as a readable page, every year. A "Chapters" button stays at the top for moving around. Each chapter is a short heading with one phrase circled by hand, two paragraphs and the numbers as large badges ("921 samples processed", "110 coffee releases"). The prices it pays are drawn against the market benchmarks on one chart. Staff tenure, retention and the amounts given by each fund are printed in full. Purple, orange, coral and lime blocks with a heavy grotesque and an italic serif.

        Eleva takes: Trust and legal: a yearly "How Eleva works" page with chapters: how many experts applied and how many were accepted, what is checked, what Eleva keeps from a booking and what the expert receives, how refunds went, how data requests were handled. Numbers as badges, one chart, chapter navigation.

        Not to copy: Not the design the jury saw. The page is about 24,700px long; the capture holds the first 12,000px. The colours are saturated and change every screen; Eleva would use one calm palette.

        Honest limits

        What this pass did not cover

        • Video call room and waiting room, emails, the help centre (apps/docs), admin, team and academy apps were not audited in this pass.
        • Open mega menus, the cookie banner and its preferences dialog, the choose-how-to-meet step, and error states (slot taken, hold ended, payment failed) were not captured; D0.3 adds them.
        • The demo member has no bookings, so a booked member's home, session detail and report were judged from source, not screens; D0.1 fixes that.
        • Dark mode and PT/ES layouts were not captured. Captures are English, light theme.
        • No accessibility tooling (axe, screen reader) was run; a11y notes come from looking at the captures.
        • Findings marked for legal review are design proposals. The panel did not give legal advice.
        • Mobbin had no women's-health marketplace and no clinician licence check; those references come from other domains and are used for structure only.
        • The content pages (newsletter, podcast, community, evidence-based care, contact, history) have references and judging criteria but no captures or findings yet; D8.3 captures them first.
        • The three brand directions are proposals from references. None has been tested with members, and the motion ideas have no reference behind them because stills cannot show motion.
